## Pricing

## Questions? We have answers

*   
How is AI visibility measured in Ahrefs Brand Radar?

Brand Radar measures AI visibility by running 451M+ search-backed prompts through AI platforms (AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot) and storing every response. Your visibility is then calculated from [how often your brand is mentioned or cited in those responses, with these key metrics:](https://help.ahrefs.com/articles/11064852-about-brand-radar)

    *   Mentions – how often your brand name appears in AI answer text

    *   Citations – how often AI links to your pages or domains as a source

    *   AI Share of Voice – the percentage of AI responses within your topic set that mention or cite your brand versus competitors

    *   Estimated Impressions – potential visibility weighted by the real search volume behind each prompt

*   What’s the difference between the AI Visibility Index and Custom Prompts?

The AI Visibility Index maps how brands appear across millions of pre-collected AI responses, instantly, with no setup. It’s ideal for benchmarking share of voice and discovering topics you didn’t know AI was answering. It works best for established brands or topics with meaningful search demand, since the index is built on Ahrefs’ keyword database and may have limited coverage for brands with little or no search volume.

[Custom Prompts](https://ahrefs.com/ai-prompt-tracking) are specific buyer questions answered by the AI platforms that matter to your pipeline, defined and set up by you, populated with data from the moment you start tracking. Brand Radar runs them on demand as often as daily. They are great if your brand is not well-known, or you have uncommon queries to track.  
*   
How does Ahrefs Brand Radar collect AI visibility data?

Brand Radar builds two distinct kinds of indexes:

    *   Prompt-based indexes (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, AI Overviews, AI Mode). [Ahrefs takes real queries from its keyword database](https://ahrefs.com/blog/brand-radar-methodology/), expands them into natural questions via People Also Ask and semantic fanout, then runs the resulting 451M+ prompts through each AI platform and stores the responses.

    *   Search-query-based indexes (AI Overviews and AI Mode only). Instead of asking AI a question, these track the keywords that trigger an AI answer inside Google Search, and whether your brand appears in it. They exist only for AI Overviews and AI Mode, because those are the only AI surfaces that show up in Google’s own results.

Question sets are re-tested monthly on a 90-day reporting window. Because both index types derive from real search demand, not synthetic guesses, the visibility metrics reflect what people really ask.

*   
What kind of queries can I track in Ahrefs Brand Radar?

Brand Radar tracks AI visibility across two query types, filterable by platform:

    *   Prompts – long-tail natural-language questions available for ChatGPT, AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, and Claude.

    *   Search queries – short queries that triggered an AI answer in Google (via AI Overview or AI Mode). Brand Radar tracks whether your brand appears in it. This type only covers AI Overviews and AI Mode, because they’re the only ones that show up inside Google Search.

*   
Can I backtrack my AI visibility data to my SEO strategy?

Yes. Every prompt in the Index maps back to real search demand, on two levels:

    *   Search demand – the branded keywords behind your mentions, so you can see the actual query volume driving your AI visibility.

    *   Topics – clustered keywords that group related queries, so you can see which high-volume topics trigger AI answers, which pages and domains get cited, and where your content is (or isn’t) feeding AI responses.

Brand Radar also tracks the social channels that influence AI answers (Reddit threads ranking in Google and YouTube).

*   Do I need to set anything up or wait for data to collect?

For the AI Visibility Index, you don’t have to set anything up. You can immediately search any brand, product, or entire category, including historical responses back to 2025, and no domain cap.

If you choose Custom Prompts, you have to configure them yourself. The data starts to accumulate from that point. You can choose the checking cadence from monthly to daily per AI platform.  
*   
How fresh is the data, and which platforms are covered?

The AI Visibility Index covers:

    *   AI Overviews

    *   AI Mode

    *   ChatGPT

    *   Perplexity

    *   Gemini

    *   Copilot

Its question sets are re-tested monthly on a 90-day reporting window (Search Demand refreshes every few days, Web Visibility every few minutes).

Custom Prompts supports all of the above plus Claude. You pick the tracking cadence per platform (daily, weekly, or monthly), so you can spend your checks where freshness matters most. Every paid [Ahrefs plan includes a daily Custom Prompts quota](https://ahrefs.com/ai-prompt-tracking) (Lite 5, Standard 10, Advanced 20), with larger check-based packages available.

#### Have other questions?

If you have more questions, [contact us](https://help.ahrefs.com/) so we can help.

kept.heading: 60-70% OF INFLUENCER BRIEFS NOW FAVOR MID-TIER CREATORS AS BRANDS QUESTION COST OF MEGA INFLUENCERS (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Brands are favoring mid-tier creators as engagement and measurable performance matter more than follower count. Creators with 50K–500K followers can deliver lower CPVs, while historical views, watch time, and audience fit increasingly shape pricing decisions. Mega creators still command premiums when they offer mass reach or cultural relevance, but brands are pushing for fees that better reflect expected campaign performance.

# 60–70% of influencer briefs now favour mid-tier creators as brands question cost of mega influencers

## The shift is being driven by brands scrutinising what they get back for every rupee spent on influencer marketing, with engagement, cost per view, watch time and conversions increasingly carrying more weight in creator selection.

By [**Indrani Bose**](https://www.storyboard18.com/author/indrani_n18)|September 21, 2026, 08:01:01 IST

[Choose Storyboard18 on](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=storyboard18)

Follow

Share

![Image 11](blob:http://localhost/4e7f29d31e0a881c07160b69a3c08401)![Image 12: 60–70% of influencer briefs now favour mid-tier creators as brands question cost of mega influencers](https://images.storyboard18.com/storyboard18/2026/09/Kuku-Technologies-gets-SEBIs-green-light-for-confidential-IPO-filing-4-2026-09-7a95ceb4b5cf000114663600a9b0bc0a-1019x573.jpg)

But creators with something that is difficult to replicate — celebrity value, cultural relevance, a distinctive IP or a particularly trusted community — can continue to charge a premium. 

ADVERTISEMENT

Brands are increasingly shifting influencer marketing budgets towards mid-tier creators as advertisers demand stronger returns, predictable views and measurable business outcomes instead of paying a premium simply for follower count.

**Sonia Sarashetti, Deputy Managing Director at Barcode Entertainment**, said roughly 60–70% of the briefs the agency now receives show a strong preference for creators with between 50,000 and 500,000 followers.

The shift is being driven by brands scrutinising what they get back for every rupee spent on influencer marketing, with engagement, cost per view, watch time and conversions increasingly carrying more weight in creator selection.

“The conversation has moved beyond reach as a standalone metric. Mid-tier creators often bring stronger community affinity, better engagement and, importantly, a perception of greater authenticity,” Sarashetti said.

### Trending Topics

[OpenAI](https://www.storyboard18.com/digital/openai-unveils-jalapeo-ai-chip-with-broadcom-as-it-moves-deeper-into-ai-hardware-108866.htm)[nestle ceo](https://www.storyboard18.com/advertising/nestle-sees-india-as-a-top-5-global-market-by-revenue-ws-l-108868.htm)[AI Tech Jobs](https://www.storyboard18.com/trending/ai-is-replacing-some-jobs-but-these-12-new-ai-jobs-are-emerging-fast-100513.htm)

Rather than placing a large part of a campaign budget behind one creator, brands can also use a wider pool of mid-sized creators to build reach across different audiences.

The economics are beginning to show up sharply in campaign performance.

According to Sarashetti, mid-tier creators can deliver cost per views (CPVs) of below ₹0.30 on several campaigns, compared with ₹0.80 or more for larger creators. Celebrity-led or premium creator integrations can see CPVs cross ₹1.50.

Mid-tier creators can also deliver engagement rates above 3%, she said.

“For us, the bigger shift is that brands are beginning to look at the cost of meaningful attention, rather than simply the cost of access to a large audience,” Sarashetti added.

**Follower count no longer enough to justify the price**

Opraah is seeing a similar change in how advertisers build campaigns.

“Brands aren't abandoning mega creators; they're just tired of paying for empty reach,” said **Pranav Panpalia, Co-Founder, Opraah**.

Panpalia said mid-tier creators have increasingly become the preferred choice when campaigns require niche communities, audience trust or trackable conversions. Larger creators, however, continue to play a role where brands want immediate mass reach or broad cultural visibility.

“If a brand wants performance, I'd take a creator with 200,000 hyper-engaged followers who trust their word over a 2-million-follower account where 80% of the audience is passive,” he said.

The change does not mean the premium commanded by million-plus creators has disappeared altogether. But brands are demanding greater proof that the audience attached to those follower numbers will actually deliver.

Sarashetti said follower count remains valuable for campaigns seeking immediate scale or a recognisable face, but brands are becoming less willing to pay large premiums without clear expectations on performance.

“We are seeing more conversations around deliverables, expected views, watch time, engagement benchmarks and, in some cases, performance-linked structures,” she said.

Larger creators are consequently having to justify pricing through campaign outcomes rather than relying on audience size alone.

Panpalia echoed that shift, saying follower numbers that once gave creators considerable pricing power are now being weighed against average views, audience demographics, retention and the volume of sponsored content appearing on their feeds.

“Follower count used to buy you a blank check; today, it barely buys you a meeting,” he said.

Deals are also becoming more complex, with conversations increasingly covering usage rights, exclusivity and performance incentives.

**Brands look at what creators can actually deliver**

Expected views are now becoming a baseline in campaign negotiations, though neither executive believes follower count has stopped mattering entirely.

At Barcode, brands are increasingly comparing creators against their historical performance, alongside expected and actual views, watch time, engagement quality, audience relevance and conversions.

“So the question has evolved from ‘How many followers does this creator have?’ to ‘What can this creator realistically deliver for this investment?’” Sarashetti said.

At Opraah, the evaluation can vary depending on the campaign objective.

For e-commerce campaigns, revenue and cost per acquisition can become central metrics. Brand-awareness campaigns are more likely to prioritise unique reach and attention time. Brands are also examining average views, completion rates, geography, age, category affinity, saves, clicks and previous campaign conversions before signing creators.

Panpalia said predictive tools are increasingly being used to estimate views and business outcomes before campaigns go live.

**Too many ads can hurt creator value**

The rethink is also forcing advertisers to pay closer attention to creator overexposure.

Both executives said a high volume of brand partnerships can weaken the very audience trust advertisers are trying to buy.

“Overexposure is becoming a real consideration, particularly for creators who work across a very high volume of brand partnerships,” Sarashetti said.

As audiences become better at distinguishing paid endorsements from genuine recommendations, brands are looking at how often creators advertise, the categories they endorse and whether a partnership fits naturally with their content.

Panpalia described overexposure as a “brand safety risk”, arguing that advertisers need to examine a creator's ad-to-organic content ratio and existing brand clutter before making a selection.

“Three deeply integrated, authentic brand partnerships will drive significantly more long-term value than ten rushed ads slapped onto a cluttered feed,” he said.

The emerging divide is therefore less about big creators versus small creators and more about whether a creator can justify the cost attached to their audience.

For advertisers, follower count is increasingly becoming the starting point of the conversation — not the final measure of influence.

# Why I Am Bullish on ChatGPT Ads

September 17, 2026  by Vincent Schmalbach

I have done SEO for more than twenty years, since Google was the new search engine, and I ran Google Ads campaigns back then too. So I have watched a search company build an ad business once before. Ad-supported ChatGPT is going to work, and I am bullish on it.

I'm writing this while working on [vroni.com](https://www.vroni.com/?utm_source=vincentschmalbach.com&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=blog_post_vroni&utm_content=inline_note), my AI coding tool for turning tasks into pull requests.

The numbers already point that way. OpenAI started testing ads in the US on February 9 for Free and Go users, and by August 31 it reported that [ChatGPT Ads had reached $1 billion in annualized revenue in under 200 days](https://openai.com/index/expanding-access-to-ai-with-chatgpt-ads/), with tens of thousands of advertisers, availability in over 40 countries, and self-serve buying in [31 European markets](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-across-europe/). But the revenue is not why I am bullish.

In February 2002, Google switched AdWords to cost per click and [ranked ads by a combination of click-through rate and the price the advertiser agreed to pay](http://googlepress.blogspot.com/2002/02/google-introduces-new-pricing-for.html). You picked keywords, you set your bid, and what you paid depended on who else was bidding, what they bid, and how often people clicked each ad. An ad nobody clicked lost its spot no matter how much money was behind it. The ads sat in their own column next to the results, and the press release promised that the organic results were "unaffected by payment". I think that was the best advertising system ever built. It worked for advertisers, and it worked for users. Today everyone hates everything to do with ads, but back then the ads were a feature. They were relevant, I clicked plenty of them myself and found what I was looking for, and you could always choose to look at the results or look at the ads, instead of the commingled mess we have now.

If ChatGPT ads become anything like that, I am all in. On paper, that is what OpenAI is describing. Its stated principles say [ads are "always separate and clearly labeled" and "do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you"](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-advertising-and-expanding-access/), the first format is an ad at the bottom of an answer when there is a relevant sponsored product, and Plus and Pro stay ad-free. Free users can even [opt out of ads in exchange for fewer daily messages](https://openai.com/index/testing-ads-in-chatgpt/). I do not know what the final format should look like, but a labeled ad below an answer that was written without the ad in mind is the 2002 shape, not the 2026 Google shape.

Meanwhile Google is trying to become ChatGPT. At I/O in May it announced [the biggest change to its search box in 25 years, "completely reimagined with AI"](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/search-io-2026/), with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the default model in AI Mode. When the incumbent starts copying the newcomer, the original usually wins. Most people still use Google because it is what they know. Many of them do not think of ChatGPT as an alternative at all. But think back to using AltaVista or HotBot and then running your first Google search. It was obvious within seconds that Google was better, faster and more accurate, so you switched and never went back.

You want an answer, so you ask Google, because that is what you know. But those answers are not good. People expect Google to be instant, and by Google's own count it handles [more than 5 trillion searches a year](https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/ai-personalization-and-the-future-of-shopping/). If you want an AI answer on that many queries, delivered instantly, you cannot run a strong model. You run the fastest and cheapest one you have, and I think that is why the default in AI Mode is a Flash model. So the answer leaves a bad taste. You read it and think, that cannot be right, and then you find out it was wrong. At some point someone says, why did you not ask ChatGPT, and you try it, and the answer is much better.

That gap did not exist a year ago. Back then, normal ChatGPT web search summarized the top ten results for you, roughly what Google's AI Overview does. The alternative was deep research, which OpenAI launched in February 2025 on [a version of o3, at 5 to 30 minutes per query and 100 queries a month on the $200 Pro plan](https://openai.com/index/introducing-deep-research/). It was excellent, and people were rightly excited about it, but you used it for serious research, not as a replacement for a web search. A year ago I would ask ChatGPT about a topic I wanted to understand, and I would still go to Google when I needed new running shoes.

That has completely changed. I use a paid account and only the Pro models and features, so I cannot speak for the free version, though since August the free tier has [run GPT-5.6 Luna with unlimited text chats](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/openai-brings-unlimited-chatgpt-text-chats-to-free-users/) which is a rather good model. If I ask ChatGPT a question I would have typed into Google, it scans the web, investigates, and does the thinking for me. It goes deeper than a summary. It is as skeptical as I am, so when it hits SEO spam or an astroturfed Reddit thread, it dismisses it and moves on. It can search, scrape and use websites, so it can find the best running shoe, the best places to travel, or the cheapest price for something. It is still not instant. I wait 10 to 20 seconds for that kind of answer, and either I get used to that or ChatGPT gets faster. But when I want to research anything now, ChatGPT is the place, not Google.

Running shoes, travel destinations and price comparisons are exactly the queries ads work on. In March 2025 I wrote about [the chatbot monetization problem](https://www.vincentschmalbach.com/the-chatbot-monetization-problem-can-ai-chatbots-be-as-profitable-as-google/), where chatbots got the informational questions while Google kept the profitable commercial ones. That has flipped. The commercial questions are moving to ChatGPT, because ChatGPT answers them better.

The objection I hear is that once ads exist, they will creep into the answer itself, and you will never know whether you are being sold something. I get that, and it is a valid concern. It is also exactly the concern people had about Google from the start and still have. It is a conflict of interest. I am not going to judge how well Google has handled it, or how well OpenAI will. What I can say is that it has not hindered Google's economic success at all, and I do not think it will hinder ChatGPT's either.

Title: 10 unconventional ways to brag about your customers 🌈

URL Source: https://www.marketingideas.com/p/10-unconventional-ways-to-brag-about

Published Time: 2026-09-21T07:08:19+00:00

Markdown Content:
_**Today’s ✨ free marketing idea ✨ is sponsored by enso**_

800M+ people ask ChatGPT what to buy every week. ChatGPT sells ad slots in those answers now, and almost no marketer is buying them. I don’t say this often, but if you’re going to try one new channel this year - it should be this one.

**[enso](https://www.enso.bot/chatgpt-ads)** is a growth hacking lab and an approved ChatGPT Ads partner. Their agents run the whole thing: creative, targeting, measurement.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!88_A!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F541718cc-ae80-4d8b-a69f-160a0ae32e1a_1600x837.jpeg)](https://www.enso.bot/chatgpt-ads)

The best part: Join enso as a customer before September 30th and get $10,000 in ChatGPT Ads credits (for free)!

[Get $10,000 in ChatGPT Ads credits →](https://www.enso.bot/chatgpt-ads)

_→ [Sponsor my newsletter](https://forms.gle/KFS6X5EEeQtWqte87)_

You’ve seen the boring “Trusted by” logo row 10,000 times.

Which is a waste, because your customers are the best proof you have.

I’ve been collecting companies that show off their customers in ways people actually STOP and look at. Here are the best 10 ideas I found:

Look at the homepage of [Deel](https://deel.com/), a payroll tool for global teams.

“Trusted by 40,000+ companies... and **EVEN SNOOP DOGG**”. When you hover over the logos - you reveal a secret button:

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jyuV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F426f297c-1a48-4d03-a08b-e8d397b61c53_1000x332.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jyuV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F426f297c-1a48-4d03-a08b-e8d397b61c53_1000x332.gif)

Snoop Dogg is a “real” customer (his ice cream company hires through Deel), and the button opens a [funny case study](https://www.deel.com/snoop/) about it.

**How to steal this:** do an influencer deal where the deliverable is a funny story about the star being a “customer” of yours. A weird customer in the row makes people stop and look at all the other logos and case studies.

Notion gives away the [Figmanual](https://www.notion.com/templates/collections/case-study-use-templates-like-figma), Figma’s internal handbook, as a template:

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8NzH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf8ab9c0-d199-4cdc-a1dc-67e3ca371fa2_2964x1820.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8NzH!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf8ab9c0-d199-4cdc-a1dc-67e3ca371fa2_2964x1820.png)

It’s a brag and a lead magnet at the same time. Figma runs its company on Notion, and to get Figma’s handbook, you need a Notion account.

**How to steal this:** ask your best-known customer for permission to publish the thing they built on your product (a checklist, a dashboard, a workflow) as a free template with their logo on it.

Hinge is a dating app.

They asked **16 authors** to interview real couples who met on the app and write their love stories - now it’s printed books, a [Substack](https://www.no-ordinary-love.co/), and an audiobook:

[![Image 4: Hinge book](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b842!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d564c48-44cf-44ef-a36d-89d31bcd08e8_1200x630.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b842!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d564c48-44cf-44ef-a36d-89d31bcd08e8_1200x630.jpeg)

**How to steal this:** interview a customer and write it up as a novel-style story with their photo, then send them the PDF to post. (With a budget, I’d print it as an illustrated kids’ book and mail it to their team.)

Stripe’s billboards brag about Stripe’s customers. I took this photo in Times Square last year:

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zDEv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F752e93bd-d173-4365-9046-1af3fd2c0e09_1200x1468.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zDEv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F752e93bd-d173-4365-9046-1af3fd2c0e09_1200x1468.png)

The focus is on their customer Instacart. Stripe is tiny on the bottom.

**How to steal this:** write the next post entirely about one customer’s win, and barely talk about yourself. With a few hundred dollars, [Blip](https://www.blipbillboards.com/times-square/) (a website that sells digital billboard slots) can put that post on a screen next to the customer’s office for 1-2 minutes, and the customer will probably post the photo if you tell them when to look.

Shopify did the same thing for its smallest customers.

For Black Friday 2024 it put a live map of orders on the Las Vegas Sphere - and every firework is a merchant’s **first sale ever**:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZXpm1X7-PFM)

I love it.

We do it at Wiz with our **Zero Critical Club** (the first win in our product is reaching zero critical issues in their environment):

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!64jG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda84322c-29c8-49a0-aa16-4a3658018c31_1012x912.png)](https://lnkd.in/p/gd7uH367)

**How to steal this:** you don’t need budget for this one. The next time a customer gets their first win with your product → post it on LinkedIn with them tagged.

Snowbird is a ski resort in Utah.

They took a real one-star review - “**Too advanced**“ - and made it the [ad](https://www.struck.com/work/snowbird-one-star/):

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!f_rq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d4744d5-0410-4c2c-9d2f-755469bb4b3b_2398x1632.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!f_rq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d4744d5-0410-4c2c-9d2f-755469bb4b3b_2398x1632.png)

A bad review from the wrong customer is a compliment from the right one.

**How to steal this:** find the one-star review that says you’re “too” something your best customers love (too strict, too simple), and put it on your homepage.

Every customer logo on [Clay](https://www.clay.com/)’s homepage comes with a result, e.g. Intercom’s says “**+140% outbound pipeline**“:

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LBkv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F09ecf729-f3c9-4828-a5b5-972dc5f7cafb_2490x794.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LBkv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F09ecf729-f3c9-4828-a5b5-972dc5f7cafb_2490x794.png)

**How to steal this:** email each customer whose logo you show and ask for one number you can quote. A number under the logo tells visitors it worked.

The only thing better than showing numbers → is to also give the proof they’re real.

[Greptile](https://www.greptile.com/customers) is an AI tool that reviews code. Its customers page lists **real bugs it caught** in well-known open-source projects, each one linked to the actual fix on GitHub:

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!e63t!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F341303bc-cba0-46ba-a802-ff03b532c0eb_2770x2298.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!e63t!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F341303bc-cba0-46ba-a802-ff03b532c0eb_2770x2298.png)

People believe what they can check themselves.

**How to steal this:** next to every customer logo, link to the actual thing your product did for them: the website you built, the ad you wrote, the email they sent with your tool, or the bug you caught.

Red Wing makes work boots.

Their flagship store has a [wall of boots](https://www.redwingshoes.com/stories/wall-of-honor/) that real customers wore through **a working lifetime**, with their stories:

[![Image 10: The Wall of Honor with all the honoree's boots hanging on the wall with their plaques next to them](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!62Ee!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F32bb5d14-1f64-416d-a57a-40f40aa46c58_1920x756.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!62Ee!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F32bb5d14-1f64-416d-a57a-40f40aa46c58_1920x756.webp)

**How to steal this:** put “Customer since [year]” under every logo. A customer who stayed 6 years says so much more about you than a new big-name logo.

[Pylon](https://www.usepylon.com/) is a customer-support tool.

Earlier this year, they grouped their customer logos by the competitor each one left - “**Migrated off** Zendesk”:

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOyz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedec251b-35f4-43c1-8fb4-8bffe4678508_2811x1196.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOyz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedec251b-35f4-43c1-8fb4-8bffe4678508_2811x1196.png)

[Rent the Runway](https://www.renttherunway.com/product_reviews/MDW287) does it with people. Every dress review shows the reviewer’s **size, height, weight, and body type**:

[PostHog](https://posthog.com/) (an analytics tool) made the grouping a funny game. You can reshuffle its logos into categories, like **companies you can explain to your parents** vs. companies you can’t:

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TQx2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59c76348-4242-48f2-8fcd-a8d2ffd67421_2186x944.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TQx2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59c76348-4242-48f2-8fcd-a8d2ffd67421_2186x944.png)

**How to steal this:** split the logos you already have into 2 or 3 groups and let the labels brag (”Switched from [Competitor]”, “Under 50 employees”). Visitors look for a customer like them, and the label helps them find one.

One last thing - and it’s the most painful mistake I’ve seen this year:

See you next week ✌️

Tom

Title: Great products need great stories

URL Source: https://quietmoats.substack.com/p/great-products-need-great-stories

Published Time: 2026-09-20T19:57:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z3ja!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6989b41-41d4-4f67-b040-72fcfc1f2ee6_3024x3024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z3ja!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6989b41-41d4-4f67-b040-72fcfc1f2ee6_3024x3024.jpeg)

I read a fair amount of computer history. And one thing you start to notice, if you read enough of it, is how often it undermines one of the most widespread beliefs in tech today: that the better product wins.

Quite often, the better product doesn’t win—at least not by itself. You can welcome something into the world that is objectively better—faster, more performant, capable of things that were previously impossible—and still watch it languish, never quite finding product-market fit.

In tech, we’d call this a distribution problem. But I’ve come to believe this diagnosis is far too coarse. In many cases, I think it’s better understood as a problem of imagination.

The underlying reason: a new frontier can exist for years and still feel irrelevant to most people, simply because it's hard for them to picture themselves there. What draws people to the frontier, by and large, isn’t the frontier itself. It’s some vision of who they might become, or how they might live, once they get there. Someone has to supply that vision, and it rarely comes from the people still deciding whether to make the trip. If computer history teaches anything, it’s that great builders, at some point, have to put down their tools and become great storytellers.

My favorite example of this is the Apple II.

When it launched in 1977, the Apple II was unusually approachable for a computer of its time. At a moment when many personal computers were still sold as kits that hobbyists had to solder together themselves, the Apple II was one of the first to arrive as a finished product: fully assembled, with a built-in keyboard, ready to use out of the box. Today we take much of this for granted, but back then, it was a genuine break from how computers were manufactured. By decoupling using a computer from knowing how to build one, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak made personal computing accessible to a much wider audience.

And yet, despite being easier to use and more polished than almost anything else on the market, the Apple II sold very modestly at first. The issue wasn't the computer itself; rather, it was that most people still found it difficult to answer the simple question: what would I actually do with one of these?Said differently, there was no clear story for why a computer belonged in their lives in the first place.

But this changed two years later, in 1979, when [Dan Bricklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Bricklin) and [Bob Frankston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Frankston) released [VisiCalc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisiCalc). Short for “visible calculator,” VisiCalc was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers—in other words, it was the Microsoft Excel before Microsoft Excel. Bricklin conceived of VisiCalc as a student at Harvard Business School, where financial models were still worked out by hand on paper ledgers. VisiCalc, by contrast, could update an entire model instantaneously. Now, a small-business owner could sit down, ask questions of their numbers, and get immediate answers. What if we raise prices 5 percent? What if labor costs climb? What happens to our margins if sales slip? For many people, it was the first time they could imagine what a computer might do for them.

Crucially, VisiCalc for its first year ran only on the Apple II. The story goes that business owners would walk into stores to buy the $100 VisiCalc, learn that it required the roughly $2,000 Apple II (or, ~$9,200 in 2026 terms), and simply add the computer to their order. Helped along by VisiCalc, Apple's annual sales grew from under $1 million in 1977 to $118 million by 1980. That December, Apple would go public in the biggest IPO since the Ford Motor Company.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NM49!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74e173d9-73f6-4c4f-ade9-614104e1a9ba_1024x796.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NM49!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74e173d9-73f6-4c4f-ade9-614104e1a9ba_1024x796.jpeg)

Steve Wozniak (left) and Steve Jobs (right) ([Source](https://computerhistory.org/blog/apple-ii-dos-source-code/))

What the story of VisiCalc demonstrates is that the further out a product sits on the frontier, the harder it is for most people to imagine themselves using it. Great products, whether founders like it or not, need great stories.

Steve Jobs understood this better than most. Responding to an audience question at Apple's 1997 developer conference, [Jobs said this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oeqPrUmVz-o):

> You’ve got to start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology…

Reflecting on it now, this principle feels especially timely, particularly as artificial intelligence pushes the frontier at breakneck speed. AI, I worry, is moving faster than our ability—or perhaps our willingness—to explain who it is for and what it makes possible.

I’ve noticed this gap most clearly whenever I leave San Francisco. Words that are tossed around here every day—like tokens, sub-agents, context windows, and Astra—mean almost nothing to my friends back home. I suspect they probably mean just as little to folks in other parts of the country.

From inside the SF bubble, it can be tempting to write off anyone who doesn't speak this language as afraid of change, resistant to technology, or doomed to enter the [permanent underclass](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/30/opinion/ai-labor-work-force-silicon-valley.html). But I don’t think this is right. My read is that most people aren't afraid of the future; they just can't see themselves in the one we keep describing.

Often, I find myself thinking about this whenever Tesla comes up.

Whatever you think of Elon Musk (and you probably think something), Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD) is generational technology. Cars that drive themselves were the dream of science fiction for much of the last century, and now these cars are actually on the road. And yet I'm surprised, and quite candidly, a little sad by how many people I meet who have only the vaguest sense of what FSD is. Most know Tesla has some kind of self-driving feature, but few could tell you what it feels like to use, or what it fundamentally changes about driving. While the technology itself has advanced at a remarkable clip, the public imagination around it still feels oddly underdeveloped.

[![Image 3: Tesla's Full Self-Driving Blew Me Away. I Still Wouldn't Buy It](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kA6Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe87d5988-4e86-4c84-b80f-9205f1fe1421_1920x1920.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kA6Z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe87d5988-4e86-4c84-b80f-9205f1fe1421_1920x1920.webp)

Tesla’s Full Self-Driving ([Source](https://insideevs.com/reviews/781325/tesla-full-self-driving-review/))

Part of the problem, I think, is its story. If you look at Tesla's [FSD page](https://www.tesla.com/fsd), it's almost entirely about the product’s technical capabilities: its cameras; parking features; safety systems. As you scroll, the emphasis stays squarely on how impressive the technology is, while notably very little real estate is given to the new possibilities it opens up.

Personally, the possibility I find most intriguing is how FSD might change our relationship to distance. I have a friend who regularly uses FSD to drive from San Francisco to Los Angeles, door to door. It's the same number of miles. It takes the same number of hours. But the toll it takes on him is less. And so he makes the trip a lot more often.

That, to me, is the more compelling story. Not that the car drives itself, but that a long trip feels lighter, and less exhausting, than it used to. Maybe that means someone sees their parents more often, or visits more national parks. While the technical story here is about AI, the _human_ story is that technology has the power to shrink distance—and, at the same time, expand our radius of life.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Ssh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc735a729-4be2-4413-ada5-b44ee3563cbe_2326x1628.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Ssh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc735a729-4be2-4413-ada5-b44ee3563cbe_2326x1628.png)

The future of driving is autonomous—but is that all? ([Source](https://www.tesla.com/fsd))

But Tesla, I don’t think, is the only case of a company telling a smaller story than it could. I’ve seen this at other companies whose work I admire, like Anthropic.

Back in February, Anthropic ran a set of Super Bowl ads around [a single concept](https://youtu.be/9Kt5Rw1fA2A?si=QJXrzPsGqz1llDOs&t=3): someone asks AI a personal question and gets served a bizarre product recommendation instead. The punchline was that ads were coming to AI—that is, ChatGPT—but not to Claude.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pntc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1064488d-cde6-42e7-8b73-410aa2f2c855_1936x1069.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pntc!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1064488d-cde6-42e7-8b73-410aa2f2c855_1936x1069.jpeg)

The closing frame from one of Anthropic’s Super Bowl commercials ([Source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Kt5Rw1fA2A))

From a marketing standpoint, the bit was clever. It chalked a clean line against OpenAI, [won Anthropic the narrative in tech circles](https://x.com/signulll/status/2019135222328041754), and drove adoption—Claude jumped from [No. 41 to No. 7](https://techcrunch.com/2026/02/13/anthropics-super-bowl-ads-mocking-ai-with-ads-helped-push-claudes-app-into-the-top-10/) on the App Store.

But it also left me imagining what else the moment could have been.

The Super Bowl is one of the few cultural moments we have left where a company can command the attention of a gigantic cross-section of the country, and put a single message in front of millions of Americans, all at once. That’s an incredibly rare opportunity to have. And in February, when most Americans were still early in reckoning with the true gravity of this technology—both its gains and disruptions; how it might reorganize society at-large, and reshape the very rhythms of everyday life—the story told was: Claude doesn't have ads.

The science-fiction writer [William Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gibson) famously observed that the future is already here; it’s just unevenly distributed. I wonder if there’s another twist: the future is also unevenly explained.

Title: AI citation outreach: a Semrush & Claude workflow

URL Source: https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-citation-outreach/

Published Time: 2026-09-21T09:49:00Z

Markdown Content:
Optimizing for AI search is both an on-page and off-page effort. Your website should be accessible and optimized for AI models. And it also needs to appear on third-party websites that these models cite when answering user prompts.

This guide breaks down the AI citation outreach process step by step.

You’ll learn how to find citation opportunities in Semrush and how to automate the process in Claude Code.

## What is AI citation outreach?

AI citation outreach is the process of finding pages AI answers cite and getting your brand included on those pages.

Securing AI citations isn’t just about collecting [backlinks](https://www.semrush.com/blog/what-are-backlinks/).

When an AI answer cites a specific webpage in an answer to a prompt, it means that AI identified that webpage as authoritative, helpful, and relevant to that prompt.

The brands mentioned on the page also benefit from that authority. Because it boosts their [visibility in AI search](https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-search-optimization/). And provides important brand context that AI can reference.

## Why third-party sources influence AI visibility

Third-party websites influence [AI visibility](https://www.semrush.com/blog/ai-visibility/) because large language models (LLMs) retrieve and synthesize information from multiple sources to answer a prompt.

AI also looks at your brand’s website.

But the chances of AI mentioning your brand are higher when you appear in relevant online sources more often.

In fact, our [study with Kevin Indig](https://www.semrush.com/blog/the-ghost-citations-study/) found that 62% of AI citations don’t result in a brand mention, also known as “ghost citations.” So AI might cite your website in a response, but never mention you. The same dynamic shows up in[Google AI Overviews](https://www.semrush.com/blog/semrush-ai-overview-research/), where a brand's visibility often rests on a small number of cited pages.

This is particularly important for evaluation-stage prompts: questions buyers ask when weighing solutions.

For example, if you ask Claude “What are the best AI meeting notetakers?”, it runs a web search and reads multiple sources.

Not all of these websites are AI notetaking companies. For example, Claude used two real user reviews published on Medium. The response also references G2 ratings.

![Image 1: Search results for AI meeting notetakers with Medium articles highlighted as cited sources](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/9e/6c/9e6c0f73ddc7d4c7c7c46ef047016804/cffe2627fa603766e39c86897e957b2a/image.png)
Claude notes in its response that four brands dominate almost every comparison list: Otter, Fathom, Granola, and Fireflies.

So even though the product reviews Claude read mention many other notetakers, it recommends the four with the overall largest presence.

![Image 2: Claude compares Fathom, Granola, Fireflies, and Otter as top AI meeting notetakers, with cited sources](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/e8/38/e838f7d187f8f0843e7f27eb6a302b39/867c3d821869a3d7f5cd34aa1b81b0ec/image.png)
However, the reviews Claude pulled also contain outdated information, which impacts the quality of a brand’s AI visibility.

For example, the response claims that Granola doesn’t separate speakers. But its [product documentation](https://docs.granola.ai/help-center/taking-notes/speaker-attribution) says speaker attribution is available through speaker tags on Zoom and Google Meet.

So AI citation outreach isn’t just a strategy to [close AI visibility gaps](https://www.semrush.com/blog/find-ai-visibility-gaps-with-semrush/). You should also use it to ensure online sources provide accurate information about your products.

## How to prioritize AI citation opportunities

When prioritizing opportunities for AI citation outreach, take into account the following factors:

**Factor****Why it’s important**
Citation impact The pages you prioritize should feature frequently in AI responses across AI platforms. This is proof they are influential.
Prompt relevance The cited pages should appear in responses to prompts that are highly relevant to your brand. Such as product evaluations or issues your brand helps solve.
Competitor presence If an AI citation opportunity already features your competitors, prioritize it over pages that don’t mention any of them.
Brand gap size Does the cited page contain outdated or incorrect information about your brand? If yes, it’s a priority since it could also influence LLMs to misrepresent you.
Publisher authority Publications with industry authority carry more weight in AI responses. And your audience is more likely to trust them, too.
Outreach feasibility Some websites, like those belonging to competitors or governments, are less receptive to outreach.

Your final list of top opportunities should be feasible to implement and include [frequently cited domains](https://www.semrush.com/blog/most-cited-domains-ai/).

## How to find, win, and track AI citation outreach opportunities

To find AI citation outreach opportunities, extract the pages AI cites for your priority prompts, analyze them, then plan your outreach.

If you’re only analyzing a handful of prompts, you can do this manually in your AI visibility tracking tool.

But to do it at scale, you can use Claude Code. We’ll show you how to do it step by step below.

### Step 1: Pull citation data

The first step is to export citation data from the AI visibility tracking tool you use to monitor prompts.

If you aren’t monitoring prompts yet, you can do it in [Semrush’s Prompt Tracking](https://www.semrush.com/position-tracking/) tool. Enter your domain and click “**Set up tracking**.”

![Image 3: Semrush Position Tracking setup for hm.com with the Set up tracking button highlighted](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/ef/aa/efaafab160e50eaa0b521d7f0448ca38/cc33af77b5117626aeedfcc05275960c/image.png)
Select the AI model to track prompts in. You can choose from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google AI Mode. Add your location, then click “**Continue To Prompts**.”

![Image 4: Semrush Position Tracking targeting settings with ChatGPT selected as the search engine and United States as the location](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/05/0b/050b52bf234506409a48d64d7d85c792/5b292d361f2671a01192b6312dfd1a03/image.png)
Then, upload prompts to your campaign.

After you paste the prompts, click “**Add prompts to campaign**” > “**Start tracking**.” Wait up to 24 hours for the data to populate.

![Image 5: Semrush Position Tracking setup with H&M prompts added and the Start Tracking button highlighted](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/2c/10/2c1024d5a0e1b7d104d1ee1bd2cc1c0d/b43ed4eb967f739502f1d6a4cac8f218/image.png)
In the Prompt Tracking report, go to “Sources.” Here, you’ll find the pages AI cites in responses to your tracked prompts. And whether your brand is mentioned.

Download the list by clicking “**Export**.” Name it “sources.”

![Image 6: Prompt Tracking dashboard with Sources tab open, Export button clicked, and arrow pointing to CSV option in sub menu](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/0e/c1/0ec1dccb8db0930b823b66369fe4e12b/1a041a49bcaef93d9f24920b391768b8/image.png)
You’ll use this CSV file to run the rest of the analysis in Claude Code.

Track your AI citations

with the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit

### Step 2: Set up your Claude Code workflow

Claude Code is a version of Claude that works with files on your computer.

Although it’s a developer tool, you don't need to have coding knowledge to use it. You write your instructions in plain English, save them in a file, and Claude follows them.

Our AI citation outreach workflow in Claude Code allows you to analyze hundreds of webpages at a time. And find the best opportunities to get more AI visibility.

The workflow automatically checks whether your brand appears on specific pages and in what context, saving you hours of manual work.

Here’s how to set it up.

#### Install the Claude desktop app

Download the desktop app from claude.com/download and install it. Then launch it, sign in, and look for the “**Code”** tab.

![Image 7: Claude desktop app with the Code button highlighted for opening Claude Code](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/da/90/da906513864e2ec7190fc02328bb5f3b/4c4070e4b20a6c31993525b6e8ed1364/image.png)
You'll need a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise). Claude Code isn't available on the free tier.

#### Create your project folder

Make a new folder on your computer and name it “ai-citation-outreach.” Move your prompt tracking CSV export into it.

Then, create three plain text files in the “ai-citation-outreach” folder that tell Claude Code how to execute the workflow.

You can create these files manually using any text editor or generate them with Claude’s help.

**File****What it does**
CLAUDE.md Explains the AI citation outreach project. Claude reads it automatically at the start of every session.
brand-facts.md Your approved brand information. When analyzing outreach opportunities, Claude will check pages against this document to flag issues.
analyze-sources.md Your instructions for the citation outreach analysis. Claude will save it as a command in the “.claude/commands/” subfolder.

We’ll cover how to create these files and what they need to include in the next section.

#### Create the project files

The “CLAUDE.md” file is a project context document. It needs to explain the CSV data so Claude reads it correctly. And understands what to do.

Here’s an [example](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Zb4yOHjQ4-g5SertbDE7TdjD7eBEprAj0T-jOl8oMMM/edit?tab=t.0) using the Prompt Tracking CSV export.

Then, prepare the “brand-facts.md” file. It should include information about your:

*   Product positioning
*   Pricing
*   Available products and services
*   Direct competitors
*   Any incorrect information or claims that third-party pages often publish

And other key information that you want third-party websites to include or get right. Keep the document succinct, as overloading Claude with too much context can create confusion and slow down the process.

The file "analyze-sources.md" contains detailed analysis instructions.

Before you write it, first decide which pages Claude should skip. For example, exclude:

*   Your domain
*   Social media
*   Knowledge bases that don't take pitches
*   Directories and marketplaces
*   Vendor help centers, like help.openai.com

Handle review platforms separately. Instead of skipping them, ask Claude to write them to a second file.

And don't exclude competitor domains. A competitor's blog or comparison page might still be worth pitching.

Then, tell Claude how to categorize the pages. You can use this type of framework:

*   **Not mentioned:**The page covers your category and lists comparable brands, but you're absent.
*   **Underrepresented:**You appear, but with less depth or prominence than comparable brands on the same page.
*   **Outdated or inaccurate:** Your brand is represented, but the page contradicts your brand facts.
*   **Negative:**You appear in a critical or unfavorable framing.
*   **No clear opportunity:**The page is off-topic, doesn't cover brands like yours, or already covers you well.
*   **Manual review:**Pages Claude couldn't open or assess.

Write the file manually or with Claude’s help. Here's an [example](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11lt4zklAPuaYKppIyAbgjn0BdV_uNdM62f_6kYPqXPg/edit?usp=sharing).

Now have Claude save the file to your project folder.

Open Claude Code > “**Select folder**” > “**ai citation outreach**.”

![Image 8: Claude Code interface with the “ai citation outreach” project folder selected as the working folder](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/a1/02/a1023de0d000219ada295e7efaeca273/48d2d97747cd464ef777b2991e9408b9/image.png)
Paste this prompt, with your own instructions in place of the placeholder:

> _Create a folder called .claude/commands/ in this project, and save the following as analyze-sources.md inside it. Use the text exactly as written:_
> 
> 
> _[paste your instructions here]_

Claude will confirm once it creates the command:

![Image 9: Claude confirms creation of the analyze-sources command for analyzing cited pages and prioritizing outreach](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/73/de/73de170c6c16ca2b13b4029cb17ac0f1/8776c793a2ee31a6aeac1147b847d257/image.png)
To check the command saved correctly, type "/" in the prompt box. If "analyze-sources" shows up in the list, Claude found it and you're ready to run the workflow.

![Image 10: Claude Code command menu with analyze-sources selected to build a prioritized outreach list from cited pages](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/d6/ca/d6cafdb4221f7fed69cad35929d06799/85777b6597016065cd184213c4269209/image.png)
The file should also appear in your project folder.

This is what the completed folder looks like:

![Image 11: Claude Code project showing analyze-sources.md alongside brand facts, project instructions, and source data files](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/6b/18/6b18c24d299a71d833bcf4605f838a4b/7143032a4391fe9184eb01211ab71970/image.png)
Now, you’re ready to test the AI citation outreach analysis workflow.

### Step 3: Run the AI citation outreach analysis

To run the AI citation outreach analysis, open Claude Code, select your project folder and type “/” in the prompt box.

Select “**/analyze-sources**.” Use a more advanced model like Opus for the analysis.

Hit enter.

Claude Code will run the workflow and update you on its progress:

![Image 12: Claude reports 452 unique source URLs, applies exclusions, and leaves 330 pages for citation outreach analysis](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/af/85/af85a8e875380b85084f9b70c59504d7/8272d163765d8ec10908ae40f16b3456/image.png)
The amount of time and tokens Claude spends on the workflow depends on how many URLs are in the Sources file. (Tokens are data units that AI processes. The more data that Claude analyzes, the more tokens it uses.)

If the analysis is taking too long, you can always tell Claude to stop the workflow and resume it later at your command.

When Claude finishes, or when you stop it early, you'll get a summary of what it produced:

![Image 13: Claude summarizes citation outreach files produced, unassessed pages, and top outreach opportunities](https://static.semrush.com/blog/uploads/media/82/c4/82c49e5e8ba13be413a6a449fe4e56ea/173a6ee2f68e426ec29e95937790d287/image.png)
The workflow produces opportunities.csv (assessed pages), manual-review.csv (pages Claude couldn't open or finish), and routed-reviews.csv (review-platform pages from your exclusion rules). Open each CSV file to start the review process.

### Step 4: Review and validate Claude's output

Review the output in the “opportunities.csv” file.

Human review is non-negotiable because Claude Code can still make mistakes.

Claude is also non-deterministic. So if you run the analysis of the same file twice, you might get slightly different classifications on borderline pages.

Using our H&M example, one of the top opportunities is this roundup of the [most affordable office clothes for women](https://corporette.com/the-most-affordable-office-clothes-for-women/).

The page links to H&M twice, but Claude labeled it as “Underrepresented” and provided this explanation:

“H&M appears once (a ~$50 blazer) among ~50 brands. Expand its workwear presence, tailored trousers, blazers, and knitwear, with current price points so it reads as a fuller affordable-workwear option next to Uniqlo, Mango and Zara.”

A manual review of the page confirms Claude’s opportunity categorization. There are additional categories where the webpage could mention H&M products, but doesn’t.

Claude also missed that the article features H&M twice, in the blazer and tops sections, not once.

This is exactly why a human needs to review every opportunity. If a publisher finds an error in your pitch, they might ignore your email.

The first time you run the workflow, you might find similar errors or areas for improvement. Ask Claude to diagnose the issues in the current workflow and update the project files so future runs don't repeat the same errors.

### Step 5: Prepare the outreach handoff

Create a separate spreadsheet with a list of your human-reviewed priority opportunities. It should include:

*   The page URL
*   Associated prompts
*   Number of citations
*   Claude’s classification
*   Claude’s recommendation alongside any of your additions
*   Outreach owner
*   Date of outreach
*   Outcome

In the “Recommendation” column, provide enough context to the outreach owner so they [write a tailored pitch](https://www.semrush.com/blog/how-to-write-perfect-media-pitch/).

*   **Insufficient context:**“Add H&M to this listicle.”
*   **Sufficient context:**“H&M appears as a $50 blazer among 50 brands. Suggest adding pants and tops with current prices.”

When drafting the pitch, suggest a low-lift change instead of a long list of additions to the article.

Sean Markey, who does outreach for Semrush, found that opening with a single correction and then asking permission to send more gets a better response than leading with the full request.

Here’s an example of his pitch:

_Hi Andi,_

_My name is Sean and I'm working with Semrush._

_I'm writing about your post on how to check your Google ranking. We're in there as "SEMrush" (thanks for the mention!), but I'm hoping we can fix that to just "Semrush," plus a few other small things._

_Is it cool if I send over a quick write-up from the content team you can use to update it?_

_Thanks, Sean_

Of his last 14 responses, 8 agreed to receive the changes without asking for anything in return.

You can adapt the same structure to any opportunity type. Here’s an example using H&M:

_Hi Kat,_

_My name is [Name] and I work with H&M._

_I'm writing about your roundup of the most affordable office clothes for women. We're in there with a $50 blazer (thanks for including us!). Our prices and stock move around a fair bit, so I'd be happy to send you the current details for that piece._

_We also have a few other workwear items that would fit the post well. Is it cool if I put together a short write-up with current prices you can use to update it?_

_Thanks, [Name]_

Send a follow-up email if you don’t get a response in 3-4 days.

Some publishers might come back with a value exchange request. Before starting the outreach, align on a negotiation approach so your outreach team has a clear process to follow.

For example, you might offer:

*   A backlink, as long as your website contains pages where you can include links organically, like a blog
*   Free or discounted product access
*   A social media shoutout
*   A one-time payment. Give the outreach owner a clear budget, so they have room to negotiate

Log every ask in your outreach spreadsheet next to the opportunity.

### Step 6: Track results

Track your AI citation outreach results in the same spreadsheet you built in step 5.

Note publisher responses, implemented changes, and when they went live. Then watch what happens in your prompt tracking.

Re-export the Sources report every month and compare it to your previous export. Monitor the following:

*   Is the page still cited?
*   Does your brand now appear in the prompt responses where AI cites these pages?
*   Are new webpages appearing as citations? Do they mention your brand?

The North Star metric to track is your overall AI visibility and sentiment. Within a quarter, you should see growth in your AI response presence.

If this doesn’t happen, evaluate other aspects of your [AI brand visibility strategy](https://www.semrush.com/blog/brand-visibility/). Perhaps your product positioning and messaging is inconsistent. Or you might not have any organic content on your website that talks about what you do.

## AI citation outreach vs. traditional link building

The main differences between [link building](https://www.semrush.com/blog/link-building/) and AI citation outreach are:

**Difference****Link building****AI citation outreach**
Goal Focuses on acquiring links from high-authority websites to drive referral traffic and improve [off-page SEO](https://www.semrush.com/blog/off-page-seo/). Links from authoritative websites also help search engines see your website as authoritative, which can improve your rankings.Focuses on ensuring your brand appears on pages AI cites in relevant prompts. May include links but also incorporates important information about your brand.
Target selection Targets high-authority websites in your industry that are also relevant to your audience.Targets websites whose pages AI cites in relevant prompt responses, and where your brand doesn’t appear. Or it appears, but the information is outdated, incomplete, or negative.
Success metrics Referral and organic traffic growth, increased domain authority, improved search rankings over time.Looks at improved AI visibility in tracked prompt sets. AI referral traffic growth.
Outreach prioritization[Link building outreach](https://www.semrush.com/blog/link-building-outreach/) prioritizes opportunities based on the domain’s industry relevance and domain authority.Prioritizes outreach based on citation volume of a specific page and your visibility gap in the prompt set where the page is cited.

Even though there are differences between link building and AI citation outreach, [our study](https://www.semrush.com/blog/backlinks-ai-search-study/) with Kevin Indig and Growth Memo found that high-quality backlinks do influence AI visibility.

So investing in both is beneficial for your search and AI presence.

## Make AI citation outreach an ongoing part of your strategy

AI visibility is dynamic and requires ongoing monitoring. Now that you have a Claude Code workflow set up, it’ll be easier to perform AI citation outreach on a monthly basis.

Semrush Prompt Tracking shows you the pages AI cites for your prompts. And whether your brand appears in the answers.

Claude Code reads those pages and drafts the recommendations against your rules, which saves you hours of manual review.

But human involvement is still an essential step, especially when drafting the pitch, choosing opportunities, and [building relationships with publishers](https://www.semrush.com/blog/digital-pr-for-ai-visibility/).

Beat your competition in LLMs

with the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit

kept.heading: 5 SPICY AI MARKETING TAKES (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI is changing marketing without necessarily reducing demand for marketers. Leaner teams may be offset by the growing number of businesses needing distribution. Chat ads could become a major ad format as LLM usage grows. Shared repositories can preserve institutional knowledge and give AI better context. Employee-generated content can extend brand reach through trusted voices. As AI handles more digital interactions, IRL events may become more valuable for creating human connection and closing deals.
