kept.heading: BLOGGING STATISTICS 2026 (10 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Reported blog performance just hit an all-time low, with only 13.9% of respondents calling results strong, and the cause traces back to abandoned tactics rather than AI. Influencer collaboration, the single strongest predictor of success in the dataset at 2.6x the benchmark, has dropped from 25% of respondents in 2017 to 7% today, while original research, keyword research, and formal human editing have all declined too. AI use jumped from near zero to 92% in three years, yet users and non-users report strong results at the same rate, with only non-users skewing toward disappointing ones.
kept.article_text:
Title: Blogging Statistics 2026: What 1,042 Content Marketers Told Us About What Works [New Research]

URL Source: https://www.orbitmedia.com/blog/blogging-statistics/

Published Time: 2026-09-08T12:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Every year we ask 1000+ content marketers 24 questions. The goal is to discover what marketers create, how often, how long it takes, how they promote it, and most recently, how they use AI.

The survey includes one final, simple question: **Does your content deliver results?**

For 12 years, the answer to that question mostly held steady. Year after year, between 20% and 30% of marketers told us their blog delivers “strong marketing results.” The number bounced around a little but always stayed within that range.

This year it dropped.

![Image 1: Line graph showing percent of marketers saying blogs deliver strong results (down to 13.9% in 2026) versus those unsure if blogs deliver results (up to 18.9%), 2016–2026.](https://www.orbitmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2-The-year-the-benchmark-broke.webp)

**14% report “strong results.”** That’s six points below the previous twelve-year low. That’s a huge dip.

At the same time, **18% report “I don’t know if the blog delivers results.”** That’s a big jump. For a decade, that number always fell between 9% and 14%. Today, nearly one in five content marketers can no longer tell you whether the work they do is working.

Clearly, something happened.

**But first, the 2026 numbers at a glance…**

*   **1,312 words** – The average blog post, down from a peak of 1,427 in 2023
*   **3 hours, 20 minutes** – The average time to write one, down from a peak of 4:10 in 2022
*   **13.9%** say their blog delivers strong results, an all-time low
*   **92.4%** now use AI for blogging …and it correlates with nothing

**How to cite this research…** You are welcome to use any of these stats and charts in your content with attribution to Orbit Media. Just link back to this page. Questions? Need a custom cut of the data? Just drop us a line.

## The four eras of content marketing

The data goes back far enough to give us a unique view into the evolution of content marketing. We can break it down across four specific eras. When we step back and look at it from a distance, we can see an entire industry change its mind several times.![Image 2: Line chart showing effort (minutes per article) and results (strong reporting) in content marketing from 2014 to 2026, with effort rising then falling, while results steadily decline over time.](blob:http://localhost/0f4a9de9032093170f9a304cb896a5a5)

### 2014–2019: The arms race

In this era, everything went up together.

Time spent per post went up, climbing from two-and-a-half hours to almost four hours. Articles got much longer, rising from 800 words to more than 1,200 words. The use of email marketing nearly doubled. SEO promotion climbed eighteen percent.![Image 3: Bar chart showing average article length by year, peaking at 1,427 words in 2023, then declining slightly in 2024, 2025, and 2026. Data spans 2014 to 2026.](blob:http://localhost/9a7f7a8fb7ab6801f63d7dbfcb67f8b4)

The idea was very simple: **content marketing is a production contest, and whoever invests the most wins.**

And that playbook actually worked. “Strong results” ran 25–30% through this whole stretch. Nearly every measure of effort correlated with better outcomes. The winners were those who published longer articles, more frequent articles and spent more time on each.

### 2020–2022: Peak effort

Then the arms race topped out.

Time spent writing per article peaked back in 2022. Length peaked in 2023. Updating older articles hit a high of 73%. Content marketers were maxing out on effort and one in four reported strong results.![Image 4: Bar chart showing average time spent writing articles from 2014 to 2026; peak at 4:10 hours in 2022, then a decline in subsequent years.](blob:http://localhost/a93563f4bc23bcdbd939ece4c331e08c)

Publishing frequency changed. Marketers publishing 2–6 times per week fell from 28% in 2014 all the way down to 12% by 2022. Monthly publishing doubled. The focus was on quality, not quantity.![Image 5: Line graph showing a decline in monthly publishing and 2–6 posts per week from 2014 to 2026, with the two trends crossing in 2021; faint lines represent other frequencies.](blob:http://localhost/03da8e58f7b6cae44763a3118e694039)

The industry converged on a common strategy: **fewer, bigger, better.** And it worked. Our own correlation charts from past surveys kept showing that spending 6+ hours writing 2,000-word posts roughly doubled the odds of strong results.

But the return on investment for greater effort was flattening out. Performance stopped rising even as effort peaked. It’s just that the change was so small that none of us saw the trend.

### 2023–2025: The AI shock

Along comes AI and marketers jumped in with both feet. The use of AI went from virtually zero to 93% in just three years. That’s the fastest adoption curve in the history of digital marketing. But concerns remain.![Image 6: Bar chart showing marketers’ AI concerns in 2025 and 2026, with top worries: accuracy, originality, tone, ethics, and search penalties. Accuracy concern drops 11 points from 2025 to 2026.](blob:http://localhost/b926ec8f9d6e74e6aa486a93bc3f06f1)

With AI came speed. As we saw already, time per post has fallen four years in a row. But the big open question remains:

_“Does AI make content programs better? Or just faster and cheaper?”_

The answer is now clear.

### AI is table stakes. It doesn’t give marketers an edge.

Using AI does not improve content performance.

It certainly makes content production faster, as we just saw. We did the math and found that the average content marketer now spends 50 fewer hours writing than in 2022 (57 posts per year, 50 minutes faster per post). That’s a week of work saved. But for what? In the same period, “strong results” fell from 26% to 14%.

None of the use cases for AI in the survey correlate with performance. Marketers just got faster at making the same things.![Image 7: Bar chart showing content marketers’ reported “strong results” using AI by task; no task exceeds the 14% benchmark, with ‘write complete drafts’ and ‘suggest edits’ at 17%, and non-users at 14%.](blob:http://localhost/a3dd9f0582e52491a9691e300a0f4564)

Maybe it was an experimentation phase. Many content pros are already pulling back from the “AI for everything” era. Almost every use case for AI dropped in 2026.![Image 8: Bar chart showing percentages of content marketers using AI for various tasks from 2023 to 2026, with increasing use for “suggest edits” and “create visuals,” and declining non-use of AI.](blob:http://localhost/abc33208916c48e78b2ead2265ba523d)

Today, 92% of marketers use AI. 8% of marketers do not. Both of those groups are equally likely to report “strong results.” No difference. But non-AI users are much more likely to report “disappointing results.” These two groups have the same odds of succeeding, but very different odds of failing.![Image 9: Bar chart comparing blog results of marketers who use AI versus those who don’t, showing higher use of AI among those reporting some results and lower in groups reporting disappointing results.](blob:http://localhost/f95fde0f29b48c9ab94b43e1a95e917e)

Using AI doesn’t make you more likely to outperform. But not using AI appears to make you more likely to underperform.

So the use of AI doesn’t explain the collapse in performance. It must be something else. To find out what, we need to look at what marketers quit doing.

## Why did content performance drop?

The answer is obvious in the data. Performance dropped because content marketers are using the most effective strategies less often. Also, marketers are using the least effective strategies more often. Consider:

*   **The strategies that correlate with strong performance are ALL on the decline:** influencer collaboration, paid content promotion, faithful use of analytics, keyword research, publishing original research, using a formal editing process…
*   **The strategies that correlate with weak performance are ALL on the rise:** publish less visual content, never research keywords, publish monthly or less, replacing human editors with AI…

![Image 10: Line graph showing adoption trends of content marketing practices from 2019-2026, with “worse results” practices rising and “better results” practices declining since 2019.](blob:http://localhost/c1631125e43067c4f6d749c89ab7302d)

It’s not true that content marketing is less effective. It is true that the best approaches to content marketing have been abandoned.

* * *

![Image 11: Man with a beard and mustache, wearing a gray baseball cap and brown shirt, smiling at the camera with framed pictures in the background.](blob:http://localhost/cde38ccdffca54ca5235b5719afc6143)###### Ann Handley, [Marketing Profs](https://www.marketingprofs.com/)

_“AI makes it stupid-easy to remove effort. We all know that. But this data is a reminder that we need to be much (MUCH!) more discerning about which effort we remove, and which we keep._

_Things like publishing original research, human editing, collaboration… These aren’t inefficiencies to optimize away with our robot friends. They might look like extra steps. But they’re often where the greatest value enters the work._

_It’s a cautionary tale about the value of the long road in a shortcut world.”_

* * *

In 2026, it seems marketers are looking for shortcuts. Most marketers are doing less. It’s as if the entire industry has pulled back. There’s broad disinvestment in content despite the fact that the fundamentals still work just as well as they ever have.

This chart shows both the correlation of each approach with performance (blue text) and the decline in that approach over the last year (red bar). The reason for declining performance is clear.![Image 12: Bar chart showing percentage declines in content marketing strategies since last year; guest blogging dropped most at 29%, followed by influencer collaboration at 22%, and others shown with smaller decreases.](blob:http://localhost/a17563dcfabf9a428dc18c0ded705bb4)

Meanwhile, content marketing has gotten steadily harder over time. Over the last eight years, we’ve asked which channels are getting harder. Nothing has gotten easier since 2019.![Image 13: Line chart showing the percentage of marketers reporting increased channel difficulty from 2019 to 2026, with search, engagement, and social channels all trending upward.](blob:http://localhost/1062184356f38443b6d1344b2a7f0de4)

The problem isn’t that content marketing is less effective. The problem is that content marketers stopped doing that most effective content marketing. This is clear in the data.

## What works now in content marketing?

Here is the correlation between content strategies and marketing performance. There’s a lot of practical insight in this chart. It shows what’s working now and why a minority of content programs are still driving business outcomes.![Image 14: Bar chart showing content marketing strategies; least-used strategies like influencer collaboration and long articles yield highest rates of strong results, while common tactics deliver lower effectiveness.](blob:http://localhost/61a0c857c98547a498cca921a529f01b)

If your content program involves consistent influencer collaboration, long-form keyword-focused articles, original research reports, and webinars, you are very likely still seeing strong performance from your content program.

Let’s look at nine of the difference-making aspects of content strategies more closely…

### 1. Elbow grease still makes a difference

Marketers who put more effort into each piece are still more likely to drive marketing results, although outcomes are less certain than before.![Image 15: Line graph showing the percentage of marketers who always vs. never research keywords from 2018 to 2026, with both rates converging at about 23% in 2026.](blob:http://localhost/ed6ebdcb2b6e060ffb5a01627998b5ac)

* * *

![Image 16: Man with a beard and mustache, wearing a gray baseball cap and brown shirt, smiling at the camera with framed pictures in the background.](blob:http://localhost/cde38ccdffca54ca5235b5719afc6143)###### Mark Schaefer, [Keynote Speaker, Best Selling Author](https://businessesgrow.com/)

_“The research presents two truths and a mystery. Truths: The most effort produces the best results. The least effort produces the worst results._

_Now the mystery: In the middle range of effort, more work is not necessarily a predictor of business results. Perhaps a new class of blogger is emerging who puts in the “right” type of human work. They create unique insights and original research, but they also know how to use AI as an honest and efficient co-worker for mundane research and editing. Honestly, I believe I would be in this new category.”_

* * *

### 2. Collaboration drives performance

The most performant content marketers don’t go it alone. The most effective marketers work with experts and influencers. They pitch articles to editors, putting their content directly in front of new audiences. And they earn mentions by publishing citable research.

We are in a post single point-of-view era for content marketing.

Red bars show how many marketers do it. Blue bars show how many of those marketers report strong results.![Image 17: Bar chart comparing marketing tactics by percentage of marketers using them and those reporting strong results; collaborating with influencers leads in strong results.](blob:http://localhost/71fa2199e3840c51a4601aa99edfdd8b)

Influencer collaboration is the single best predictor of success in the dataset. Those who do it beat the benchmark by 2.6x. Sadly, it’s also the most abandoned: down from 25% of marketers in 2017 to 7% today.

Yikes. What happened to working with friendly experts?

### 3. Visual content outperforms

The more visual the content, the more likely it is to drive performance. Yet most content marketers add very few visuals to a typical piece.![Image 18: Bar chart showing that marketers using 2-3 visuals per blog post are most likely to report strong results; percentages for 1, 2-3, 4-6, and 7+ visuals are compared for two groups.](blob:http://localhost/85c132270a2c828de6f148a85e84ebd7)

Put those visuals and collaboration together and you have a piece that is filled with images and multiple points of view. What else checks those boxes? Social streams, which as we know are highly engaging. _The more your content looks and feels like a social stream, the more likely it is to perform well._

### 4. Content marketers who consider keywords outperform

SEO is alive and well. The big change is that AIs are doing searches on behalf of buyers. But the search is happening, keywords are used, and content that is easy for machines to retrieve performs well.

Not every URL is a keyword opportunity. But the content marketers who understand search, know how to measure topical demand and align pages with phrases are much more likely to report success. SEOs make good content marketers.

![Image 19: Bar chart showing frequency of keyword research by content marketers and the percentage reporting “strong results,” with highest results at “sometimes” (37%) and lowest at “always” (14%, benchmark).](blob:http://localhost/a1e22005396aa212d1f762984c636485)

Despite the fact that keyword research still correlates with performance, content marketers are less likely than ever to consider keywords in their content. This is another effective strategy that content marketers are skipping.![Image 20: Line graph showing the percentage of marketers who always vs. never research keywords from 2018 to 2026, with both rates converging at about 23% in 2026.](blob:http://localhost/ed6ebdcb2b6e060ffb5a01627998b5ac)

### 5. Some content formats perform much better than others

Blogging isn’t enough. Content can be produced in many formats and some formats perform much better than others. Unfortunately, the most effective formats are also the least common. The least effective formats are the most common.

Here again, we see the correlation between performance and the more collaborative, more visual formats. Again, red bars show how many marketers do it. Blue bars show how many of those marketers report strong results.![Image 21: Bar chart comparing content formats by publication rate and reported strong results; infographics, webinars, and roundups are most published; how-to articles rank lowest in reported strong results.](blob:http://localhost/26a4ab2f7ea5bb991375a0644fe0fca8)

### 6. Original research still outperforms

Some content programs publish new research, creating new data and statistics that didn’t exist before, making the brand the primary source for new information. This is something AI cannot do, so it’s a highly differentiated format in the era of AI generated content.

Yet content marketers have also pulled back from this strategy. After rising in popularity for nearly a decade, fewer marketers now publish new research studies, despite the fact that it improves the likelihood of performance by 50%.![Image 22: Line graph showing a decline in content marketers publishing original research, with notable drops from 2018 to 2026 and comparison between research publishers and overall marketers.](blob:http://localhost/546d6a814b7719196ef6a2413a378a81)

* * *

![Image 23: Man with a beard and mustache, wearing a gray baseball cap and brown shirt, smiling at the camera with framed pictures in the background.](blob:http://localhost/cde38ccdffca54ca5235b5719afc6143)###### **Cyrus Shepard,**[**Zyppy SEO**](https://zyppy.com/)

_“Wow. The idea that bloggers are retreating from original research is completely counterintuitive, as Google and AI engines have shifted to preferring exactly this type of content. That, and AI tools actually make original research easier to produce. While “strong results” for publishers are down across the board, happy to see research publishers fare better.”_

* * *

### 7. Human editors drive content performance

Some marketers edit their own work. Some tell AI to do it. But the marketers who have a more formal approach with human oversight are much more likely to drive performance. They have built-in defense against AI slop.![Image 24: Bar chart comparing editing methods for marketers: showing popularity and effectiveness of formal editor, multiple editors, AI edits, and informal peer review, with AI edits receiving lowest strong results.](blob:http://localhost/6a252b704b20d738d5e44fddc316ffdc)

* * *

![Image 25: Man with a beard and mustache, wearing a gray baseball cap and brown shirt, smiling at the camera with framed pictures in the background.](blob:http://localhost/cde38ccdffca54ca5235b5719afc6143)###### **Eddie Shleyner,**[**Very Good Copy**](https://www.verygoodcopy.com/)

_“Not surprising at all that the AI group reports worse results than the benchmark while the human-editor group beats it by nearly 2X. Context is everything. Nothing works the same way twice. It all depends on the current circumstances. Figuring that out is what thinking, feeling humans are good at.”_

* * *

### 8. Some promotion channels work much harder than others

Here’s yet another perfect inverse correlation between popularity and performance. The easiest and cheapest promotion channels are the least likely to drive results. The more difficult, more expensive promotion channels are more likely to drive results.![Image 26: Bar chart comparing five promotion channels by usage and reported strong results, showing least used channels like influencer collaboration and paid promotion have higher success rates.](blob:http://localhost/8b15fdb0f586c953d9b75135d62a1a7a)

### 9. Not all marketers measure

Our last popularity-vs-success correlation is about measurement. We’ve seen this every year since the inception of this research in 2014. Data-driven marketers are more likely to report success. Those who check performance are more likely to see performance.![Image 27: Bar chart showing frequency and perceived effectiveness of content analytics checks, with most frequent checkers reporting higher success and 53% unsure if their blog works. Benchmark for success is 14%.](blob:http://localhost/95e0b41228540f658a28bde95c7d84b4)

But what are marketers tracking? And how does tracking that metric correlate with results?

We asked respondents which metrics matter most, then grouped them into three categories. Here we see both the popularity of these types of metrics and the likelihood that those marketers report “strong results.”![Image 28: Bar chart showing “Traffic is the most watched metric—and the weakest,” with volume metrics most common at 39% but only 11% report strong results, below the 14% benchmark.](blob:http://localhost/8ca191aa1223fc11b92f3164599bda2c)

Traffic is still one of the most common ways to measure performance. But it’s become less meaningful in the era of AI, where buyers ask AI for a recommendation.

*   If AI recommended the brand, the buyer then clicks a citation or searches for the brand or types in the domain directly. They’re ready to act. The source of this visitor is hard to see, but the conversion rates are high.
*   If AI didn’t recommend the brand, nothing happens at all. There’s nothing to measure.

So in the AI era, [traffic goes down and conversion rates go up](https://www.orbitmedia.com/blog/conversion-rates-ai-search/).

Traffic was always an imperfect metric. It always suffered from Goodhart’s Law:

> _“When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.”_

Of course, the best marketing metrics were always in your CRM: qualified leads, deals and revenue.

## Most content programs are just blogs

We just listed eight content strategies that correlate with performance. We’ll set aside measurement because it isn’t a strategy. It’s how you know whether the others are working. So we’ll stick with eight.

_How many do you do?_

The more of those strategies you use in your content program, the more likely you are to win. Use six or more, you are nearly three times as likely to report strong results.![Image 29: Bar chart showing content marketers’ success by number of content strategies used, from 0-1 (4%) to 6 or more (39%), with a benchmark line at 14% and eight strategy types listed below.](blob:http://localhost/00aa87845105cb03ea77bfc8e62f236f)

How many respondents do all eight? Zero. None of the 1,042 respondents do them all.

_Note about Orbit’s own content program: We publish 6-8 research studies per year. All articles include many visuals and quotes from people smarter than us. Amanda edits everything before it gets published. We run monthly events: a webinar and a LinkedIn Live. We host an annual conference, Content Jam. Our program took years to build but it works like a champ._

Finally, our own reflections on content strategies after 19 years of publishing and 13 years of conducting this survey…

**Too many content programs are just blogs.** The strategy is simply to put out an endless series of text heavy, how-to articles, promoted through email and social media. They rarely use video and the content doesn’t come from a specific person.

They may write keyphrase focused blog posts, but search traffic to articles that rank for information-intent phrases has been completely torched. It will never come back to previous levels. These marketers measure traffic and they’re sad.

There’s very little creative consideration of how topics, formats and influencers combine and which combinations connect best with their specific audience.

**But a small minority of content programs do things very differently.** Influential experts are built into the program. Guest posting is built into the program. kept.heading: HOW TO USE AI TO BE MORE CREATIVE (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Refining an idea with AI made it rated 30% more creative than not using AI at all, though the type of AI feedback needs to match the idea's maturity. Mature ideas refined through AI-written text came out 18% more creative than the same ideas refined through AI-generated images. Vague ideas benefited more from AI images instead. Images make an idea feel finished and discourage further refinement, while text leaves gaps that force more imaginative thinking.

Title: How to use AI to be more creative

URL Source: https://app.sciencesays.com/p/how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative

Published Time: 2026-09-22T10:22:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
**Join us and Squarespace on our**[**live Q&A**](https://luma.com/circle-live-043?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative)**on effective social proof for your website!**

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/fff1fa36-af41-43bc-8b09-98afa4ad03c6/image.png?t=1789633828)](https://luma.com/circle-live-043?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative)

**On September 30th**, at **12pm ET / 6pm CET**, Serkan (lead research analyst on this project) and I are joining Squarespace to share the most impactful tips from the playbook, and answer - live - any questions you have.

Worth joining if you’re wondering how to use social proof on your website as effectively as you can. It’s free.

**Topic**: AI  
**For**: Both B2C and B2B  
**Research date**: June 2026  
**Universities**: University of St. Gallen, University of Lausanne

#### 📈**Recommendation**

Use AI to help you develop your ideas (e.g. a new product, an ad creative):

*   If your idea is mature (e.g. you know the storyline of your ad), ask AI to describe the final output in text

*   If your idea is still vague, ask AI to visualize it in an image

AI will help you be even more creative with your idea.

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/920692b6-601f-454b-ad85-556b4e83aaad/Insight__341__3_.png?t=1790064729)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   Scientists found that when people used AI to refine ideas, their ideas were rated (by AI and human raters):

    *   Overall 30% more creative (vs no AI use at all)

    *   18% more creative when ideas were mature and AI refined them through textual descriptions (vs images)

    *   More creative when ideas were vague, and AI helped visualize them by creating an image

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   Images make us feel like an idea is complete and final, so we [don’t think too much](https://doi.org/10.1016/0142-694X(91)90003-F?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative) about refining it.

*   However, when we read text, we have to use our imagination to fill in the gaps.

*   This makes us think [more creatively](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327957pspr1003_1?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative).

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   Experts (e.g. creative directors) might be equally creative when using AI as a visual or text-based tool, regardless of the maturity stage of the idea.

*   Scientists only tested creativity, we don’t know if that relates to higher quality ideas and results (e.g. sales).

#### 👀**Real-life example**

VizualizeAI lets people reimagine rooms in a few clicks.

❌**Issue:** They ask people to select styles but have no step where they refine ideas.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2ae78f13-cc73-4227-91df-15eac5c96af0/341_example.png?t=1789633960)

✅**Solution:**

*   Ask questions and provide textual feedback before the final output.

*   Create different user journeys for early-stage and mature ideas.

*   Recommend designers to let people [know the AI was used](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/made-with-ai-gets-lower-engagement) as part of a more complex brainstorming exercise, and not laziness as people might think.

*   Add a [disclaimer advising](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/ai-designed-hurts-sales?draft=true) designers to avoid making the use of AI the core value proposition.

#### 📖**Research**

_Remember: This is_ _a new_ _scientific discovery. In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative)_). It may also not be generalizable to your situation. If it’s a risky change, always test it on a small scale before rolling it out widely._

#### 🎁**Bonus: Trivia**

Here is how else Science Says can help you:

*   📈**Join the**[Science Says Platform](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative)to unlock all 300+ insights and exclusive playbooks

*   📘**Boost your results** with [Science-based Playbooks](https://products.sciencesays.com/?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative) (for Pricing, Ad Creatives, Ecommerce, or SaaS)

*   🔬**Get science-based content for your brand**. Publish [groundbreaking insights](https://www.sciencesays.com/enterprise-services?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-use-ai-to-be-more-creative) about AI, marketing, or management that your customers will love.

🎓 It took our team of PhDs and me **11.5****hours** to accurately turn this research into this 3-min insight.

If this was forwarded by a friend, you can subscribe below for $0 👇

kept.heading: THE BEST BRANDS MAKE THEMSELVES AT HOME (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Brands are optimising for visibility when they should be building memory. As AI makes it easier to produce more content, physical brand objects can create lasting connections that digital ads often lack. The strongest objects are distinctive enough to identify without a logo, useful or emotionally meaningful enough to keep, and rooted in something the brand genuinely owns. Starting with what a brand can make rather than what content a channel needs can lead to fewer, more memorable ideas that generate organic digital content.

Title: The Best Brands Make Themselves at Home | LBBOnline

URL Source: https://lbbonline.com/news/the-best-brands-make-themselves-at-home

Published Time: 2026-09-21T11:13:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
The advertising industry has become extremely good at making things disappear.

AI has helped to solve advertising’s production problem of making more, more quickly and across more channels. Adobe’s 2026 AI and Digital Trends Report found that 76% of organisations using generative AI have increased the volume of content they produce. Yet half of consumers give an ad, email or social post just two to five seconds to earn their interest.

That’s barely enough time to read this sentence.

We have built an industry optimised for visibility rather than memory. The challenge is no longer being seen but being kept.

Culture isn’t formed through “content” alone. It is also built through objects. Things people choose to put on a shelf, wear, carry, display, collect and pass on.

The Lego brick. The Air Jordan 1. The iPod. The Beavertown pint glass that somehow followed you home.

These objects do more than fulfil a function. They are physical expressions of the brands behind them. They create rituals, communities and stories.

“Things” have a habit of sticking around.

They sit on kitchen counters and bedroom shelves. They appear in photographs. They get borrowed, lost, repaired and found years later in the loft or at the back of ‘that’ cupboard. They become part of people’s lives rather than another interruption to them.

I’m not suggesting brands should start sticking their logo on more stuff. The world has enough tote bags.

There’s an important difference between a branded object and a brand object.

A branded object is usually something generic with an identity applied to it. Whereas a brand object could only have come from that particular brand. Its form, function and story connect to something the brand genuinely owns.

Ideally, you could remove the logo and still know who made it.

IKEA’s big blue FRAKTA bag was designed to get bulky purchases home, then became indispensable for the next ten years, carrying laundry, taking the recycling to the tip or helping move your child’s belongings when they leave for university.

Then there’s that vintage Cadbury Cocoa tin that’s been passed down the family. It hasn’t held any cocoa since 1966 but it is still doing an excellent job looking after buttons and batteries. It might appear to have disappeared into a cupboard. But every time it comes out, it brings the brand back with decades of memory attached.

Brand objects do not always need to last forever either. Sometimes their value comes from the moment they create.

With Cadbury Made to Share, we designed the chocolate bar around the everyday moments of sharing. The unequal pieces turned the product itself into the idea: who gets what, and why?

Good brand objects are easy to understand. They do not need a strategy deck or several paragraphs of supporting copy. You see the thing and get the idea.

And physical objects are not at odds with digital culture. Quite the opposite.

A distinctive object gets photographed, unboxed, demonstrated, reviewed, shared and occasionally argued over. It can generate huge amounts of content without feeling as though it was invented to fill a content calendar.

The content becomes evidence of something interesting happening in the real world.

Too often brands begin by asking what they need to make for a channel. A TikTok idea. An Instagram execution. A poster campaign.

When every idea starts with the format, it is hardly surprising that so much of the work feels disposable.

Starting with an object creates better questions.

What could this brand make that nobody else could? What might someone genuinely want to own? Could its purpose become something useful, beautiful or brilliantly unnecessary? Would anyone still care once the media spend stopped?

The answer isn’t to create more stuff. It’s to make fewer, better things. Objects with enough usefulness or emotional value to earn a place in someone’s cupboard, where every time we reach for them, the brand becomes a little harder to forget.

kept.heading: APPLOVIN GROWS 60% Y/Y ROUNDING TO $20BN IN ANNUAL PLATFORM AD SPEND (3 MINUTE READ)

kept.article_text:
Title: AppLovin grows 60% Y/Y rounding to $20bn in annual platform ad spend

URL Source: https://www.pocketgamer.biz/applovin-grows-60-yy-rounding-to-20bn-in-annual-platform-ad-spend/

Published Time: 2026-09-21T15:45:00+01:00

Markdown Content:
*   AppLovin CEO Adam Foroughi spoke at the All-In Summit 2026, discussing LLMs, personalised ads and more.
*   His mindset includes expecting "to get screwed" every day.

[**Stay Informed** Get Industry News In Your Inbox… Sign Up Today](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/subscribe/)
[AppLovin](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/industry/applovin/) CEO [Adam Foroughi](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/industry/adam-foroughi/) has suggested ads have greater potential for economic expansion compared to the rise of chatbots, even if large language models (LLMs) have greater economic value.

"What people don’t realise is just how big the mobile gaming universe has become. You’ve got over a billion people a day playing mobile casual games. These are all adults, heads of households, and the scale of the opportunity is just humongous," he said.

In January 2025, AppLovin declared that on its own platform ad spend had reached $11 billion per year. Last week, at the [All-In Summit 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JtomF4bGxHs), Foroughi shared that the company has grown 60% year-over-year, rounding to approximately $20bn.

He added that as AppLovin isn’t the only player in the marketplace, across ad companies that number is "probably more than double", leading him to estimate that around $50bn in advertising is being spent every year in the mobile games ecosystem.

**"People love the ads that we show"**

Foroughi stated the economic value of an LLM and what it’s doing in society may be greater, but that advertising is "a very profitable implementation of a deep learning model".

He argued a shift from using Google to find a product to using a chatbot won’t have a major impact on economic expansion because that same product is being sought by different means.

Conversely, presenting a relevant ad on Facebook, in an app or in-game can present users with something they weren’t aware of before. He called this a "fun moment for consumers" and a form of creating discovery.

![Image 1: yt](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/JtomF4bGxHs/hqdefault.jpg)

"You would think people wouldn’t like them, but we see tonnes of engagement on little mini-games that are appearing in other games and people are playing these previews because the technologies have gotten so good at recommending something relevant."

He noted that a lot of players watch ads because they want rewards, which creates a dynamic with the possibility of "intent". By presenting personalised ads, Foroughi suggested that experience can be further enhanced.

"If you're sitting there in a game and you're watching an ad for 30 seconds to get a free life, you're getting something that has monetary value. Now, if you're doing that, do you want to sit and watch garbage for 30 seconds or do you want to watch something relevant?" he posed.

On this basis, Foroughi argued that Apple’s increased privacy measures in recent years run counter to consumers’ actual preferences.

"If you could precisely target a user five years ago on iOS, and today someone says ‘I don't want you to precisely target me’, you group them in a bunch and you serve them a worse advertisement," he explained.

"Now, the funny outcome of that is we'll get a lot of complaints after that change that Apple made from users that say 'serve me more relevant ads - you're showing me a bunch of spam'. So, there is this notion that you need privacy regulation so that technology companies can do exactly what's expected of them. On the other side, consumers do want relevant ads."

**The value of ads and games**

Also at the summit, Foroughi revealed his mindset to making AppLovin successful, not resting on his laurels but always preparing to move quickly.

"We never think we won. We think, every day we wake up and we're probably going to get screwed right now and we better work hard. And so you've got a company that's lean with a lot of subject matter experts who are really, really focused on this thing, this mobile gaming experience, and translated into transactional behaviour on the other side," he shared.

"And so I think there's this ability to take on giants. If you're very focused, you remain lean and you can just move faster than them."

He reflected on AppLovin’s successes and challenges, on taking the company public and surviving through difficult times. In 2022, he said the company had no demand and a lot of supply. In fact, "stock went down literally every day", so AppLovin began buying back its own stock.

When shares dropped, he described an "us against the world" mentality.

![Image 2: yt](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/RyvYJkrpxHo/hqdefault.jpg)

In more recent years, AppLovin has seen its [ad revenue rise significantly](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/applovin-revenue-rises-68-to-14bn-in-q3-2025/), along with its stock price - though shares are currently below their December 2025 peak. The company has also [battled short-seller reports](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/applovin-shares-dive-19-after-latest-short-seller-report/) questioning the company's business practices.

Foroughi noted that, previously, AppLovin had bought studios and used its games business to collect data for training its first deep learning model.

As studios don’t tend to share their data with third-parties, they were bought "as a data play". Once a model that was successful in the market had been built, third-parties started coming in and AppLovin divested from its games business, [selling its studios to Tripledot](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/how-tripledots-applovin-deal-is-positioning-it-as-a-major-global-force-in-mobile-games).

Title: State of Direct Mail 2026: Consumer Insights Edition

URL Source: https://www.lob.com/state-of-direct-mail/consumer-insights/2026-report

Published Time: 2026-01-01

Markdown Content:
State of Direct Mail 2026

## Letter from the CEO

Every year, our State of Direct Mail Consumer Insights report reveals how consumer attitudes toward direct mail are changing – and what that means for marketers.

This year, one thing stands out. Economic pressure is changing not only how consumers shop, but how they use direct mail. They're looking for value, comparing offers more carefully, and holding onto mail longer as they make purchasing decisions. At the same time, they're expecting personalization that actually feels personal. Our research shows that relevance looks different across generations. The offers, messaging, and personalization that resonate with Gen Z aren't always what motivates Millennials, Gen X, or Boomers. One-size-fits-all simply doesn't work anymore.

That's the opportunity. The brands that win will be the ones that deliver timely, relevant direct mail that earns attention, builds trust, and helps people make confident buying decisions.

I hope this year's report gives you a fresh perspective and practical ways to create direct mail your customers actually want to receive.

**Ryan Ferrier**  
**CEO, Lob**

Study Methodology

Lob conducted this study in partnership with [Kirin Analytics](https://www.kelseywhiteresearch.com/)and [PureSpectrum](https://www.purespectrum.com/). The online survey was completed in July 2026 with 2,000 adult consumers across the United States, nationally representative of age, gender, income, and region.

## Key takeaways

### Price-conscious shoppers are paying closer attention to mail.

84% of consumers say rising prices have changed how they shop, and 66% say they like referring back to direct mail when considering a purchase.

![Image 1](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a8c984cbbb2cedb62a4b72c_Group%201597881840.png)

### Personalized mail looks different for every generation.

89% of consumers say relevant mail influences them to take action, but what feels relevant (and what they take action on) changes by generation.

![Image 2](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a8c988a767f50b012f75622_Group%201597881841.png)

The mailbox remains one of the few marketing moments built into everyday life.

82% of consumers collect their mail daily or nearly every day, and 87% read it the same day they receive it.

Direct mail's trust advantage is growing.

34% of consumers say direct mail feels more trustworthy than digital communication, a 9-point increase from last year.

Consumers don't mind AI. They mind experiences that don't feel authentic.

82% are comfortable with (or neutral on) brands using AI to create direct mail, but 62% say AI has made them more skeptical of digital ads + AI slop.

Direct mail sparks action beyond the mailbox.

79% of consumers have taken a digital action after receiving direct mail, and 65% have made a purchase, signed up, or become a customer because of it.

Part one: Economic pressures

## In a tight economy, consumers lean on direct mail.

Eighty-four percent of consumers say rising prices have changed how they shop. They're spending more carefully, delaying purchases, comparing options, and looking harder for real value before they buy.

This shift is changing the role of direct mail, too. Sixty-eight percent say economic conditions have changed what they pay attention to in their mailbox, with deals, affordability, and useful information taking center stage.

**Get the full picture**— hover over   
each chart to display exact values.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### “Yes, rising prices and the general economic climate have definitely shifted what catches my eye when I look through direct mail. Instead of just browsing for inspiration or new products like I might have in the past, I now immediately scan for tangible value.”

Millennial male in the Northwest

### “I pay attention to discounts, sales or special offers. Any kind of financial break I can get. I will definitely take advantage of it.”

Gen X female in the South

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

Design for the second read.

Many purchases don't happen the day your mail arrives. Make your piece useful after the first glance with side-by-side product comparisons, financing details, limited-time offers, or a QR code that saves shoppers a step when they're ready to buy.

Part two: Personalization + conversion

## The rules of personalization change by generation.

Personalization is one of the strongest drivers of conversion. Nearly 9 in 10 consumers say relevant personalized mail is what influenced them to take action. But what feels relevant? It’s not the same for everyone. Baby boomers are more likely to respond to practical shopping context, such as offers and promotions, while younger generations place greater value on basic personalization and life stage marketing. The takeaway is simple: personalization works, but only when your definition of "personal" matches your audience’s.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

Layer your personalization.

Start with the basics, like a customer's name, but don't stop there. Pair it with a timely offer, a relevant product, or messaging tied to a current need or life stage. Build campaigns around moments, motivations, and needs, not just customer profiles.

## Direct mail drives both acquisition and retention

Direct mail influences consumers throughout the customer journey. Eighty-three percent say it would encourage them to re-engage with a brand, while 48% say it makes them more likely to try a brand they've never purchased from before.

Part Three: Consumer perspectives + behavior

## Mail isn't another marketing touchpoint. It's a daily ritual.

The mailbox is one of the few marketing touchpoints built into everyday life. More than 80% of consumers collect their mail daily or nearly every day, and 87% read direct mail the same day they bring it inside. Whether driven by habit or expectation, checking the mail remains a consistent ritual across generations, creating a moment of attention that digital channels often have to fight to earn.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

Design for the mindset behind the mailbox.

76% of Baby Boomers check the mailbox out of habit, while 49% of Gen Z check because they're expecting something. The ritual is the same, but the motivation is different. Build for both: reinforce trust with consistent branding for habitual mail checkers, and reward anticipation with timely offers, exclusive content, or personalized messaging.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

## Direct mail's trust advantage is growing

Consumers still crave experiences that feel real. As digital marketing becomes increasingly crowded, direct mail continues to stand apart. This year, 34% of consumers said direct mail feels more trustworthy than digital communication, a nine-point increase from 2025. Overall, nearly two-thirds say direct mail feels more authentic, trustworthy, valuable, or memorable than digital.

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

Part FOUR: AI

## Consumers care more about authenticity than AI.

Consumers are surprisingly comfortable with AI playing a role in the creation of direct mail, especially when it's used to personalize offers, tailor content, or improve relevance. But 62% say the rise of AI has made them more skeptical of digital ads, as they encounter “slop” more frequently in online spaces.

The takeaway isn't to avoid AI. It's to use it where it adds value, then have humans make sure every campaign feels thoughtful, relevant, and worthy of trust.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### “AI makes me more cautious but also more attentive to truly personalized, relevant, and trustworthy direct mail from brands.”

Millennial male in the West

### “It makes me more skeptical of online advertising. AI has no effect on how I respond to direct marketing.”

Boomer male in the Midwest

### “If used effectively (meaning it was vetted extensively afterward) I don't have a problem. But if it's obvious and shoddy, I will think less of the brand that uses it.”

Gen X male in the South

### “AI doesn't matter to me. What matters is value.”

Gen X female in the Northeast

(Base: Half of respondents, n=1,000)

Use AI to improve relevance, then review for trust.

Tailor the offer, content, or timing, but have a human check every piece for accuracy, tone, and anything that could feel generic, confusing, or overly personal.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### What’s next? Four ways to put these insights into practice

1

Design for the decision, not just the first impression.

Consumers are taking longer to make purchases. Create mail that's worth coming back to with clear offers, comparison charts, product details, financing information, or QR codes that make it easy to pick up where they left off.

2

Personalize beyond the name field.

Names still matter, but they're only the starting point. Tailor offers, products, imagery, and messaging around what someone is actively considering, their current needs, or their stage of life.

3

Match the moment.

Not everyone opens the mailbox for the same reason. Some consumers check it out of habit, while others are expecting something meaningful. Build campaigns that fit that mindset, whether that's consistent branding that builds trust or timely, personalized offers that reward anticipation.

4

Let AI improve the experience, not replace it.

Consumers don't mind AI. They mind experiences that feel generic or untrustworthy. Use AI to improve targeting and relevance, then make sure a human reviews every campaign for clarity, tone, and credibility.

kept.heading: ADVERTISING IS GOING AI. TV ISN'T (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: By 2030, 27% of ad revenue could flow through AI-powered platforms. TV is moving slower. North American TV ad revenue is expected to grow just 3% in 2026, excluding political spending. Complex buying workflows and fragmented inventory make automation harder. AI could simplify TV buying, but it needs strong first-party data to work well.
kept.article_text:
Title: Advertising is Going AI. TV Isn’t.

URL Source: https://mikeshields.substack.com/p/advertising-is-going-ai-tv-isnt

Published Time: 2026-09-22T13:23:20+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kW7t!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c915b0d-6523-4727-9b21-fdec76274d36_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kW7t!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c915b0d-6523-4727-9b21-fdec76274d36_1024x1024.png)

I wanted to highlight a few numbers and trends that I think may not have gotten enough attention of late:

*   **27%.** That’s how much of advertising revenue Madison and Wall predicts will flow through automated AI-powered systems like Google’s Performance Max and Meta’s Advantage+ in just a few years: [$158 billion by 2030.](https://madisonandwallglobalsubscription.substack.com/p/global-advertising-growth-remains)

*   In fact, because of AI’s momentum, global ad spending is predicted to grow a whopping 11% this year, [per Madison and Wall](https://madisonandwallglobalsubscription.substack.com/p/global-advertising-growth-remains)

*   **YET** “Television advertising revenue in North America will grow by **approximately 3%**excluding political advertising in 2026”

Think about how much attention and energy is spent on CTV’s ad potential, and the billions laid out for sports rights. And yet, TV is growing a ‘less than inflation’ clip.

Then, throw in this idea. [On last week’s Marketecture podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-191-corey-ferengul-on-the-newest-start-up/id1615989259?i=1000790492578) investor Corey Ferengul spoke about the rise of [Unified Media Platforms](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/corey-ferengul-70b1_adcp-umps-share-7506692893915570176-sH6Z/), which aspired to help brands log into a single platform (have you heard that one before?) and have machines manage spending allocations for every platform that has an API.

For sure, the episode features some healthy skepticism about how quickly such platforms will be adopted, and whether they will work better for small or large brands. But their mere existence, along with Madison and Wall’s data, both point to the direction the overall ad business is headed. Brands are increasingly drawn to massive platforms that can use AI to ingest reams of data and move spending around automatically based on performance.

Madison and Wall described this as a “broader transformation visible across the North American market. Growth is not simply coming from the largest brands spending more money. More businesses are gaining access to sophisticated advertising products, while increasingly automated platforms reduce the complexity and cost required to participate.”

Where exactly is TV on that front?

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jygy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ea31b6a-3b2e-4d07-8072-dc352bdf2b8f_1300x574.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jygy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ea31b6a-3b2e-4d07-8072-dc352bdf2b8f_1300x574.png)

I asked Justin Rosen, an addressable TV veteran who’s logged stints at Comcast, Turner and Ampersand, and now leads Measurement Product at the pharma data firm IQVIA, about this issue on my[podcast this week.](https://open.spotify.com/episode/3nWZEIFp82R9spLGOAOMdr)

“In the case of targeted TV, I certainly know this to be true,” he said. “It is extremely complex. The workflows are difficult. Even in something like a more digital native environment, there’s still issues around workflow and speed. AI will fix that.”

My question is when and how. Yes, every TV sellers offers a self-serve buying option. And more companies are pushing data-driven solutions. Yet in TV, controlling and limiting inventory is still the ruling philosophy, as is fragmentation. Is there any sign that TV wants, or would allow, the kind of automated optimization that Madison and Wall is talking about - especially across competing media companies?

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oosT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81d6848e-7317-4b3a-8720-942647687e88_3300x2550.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oosT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81d6848e-7317-4b3a-8720-942647687e88_3300x2550.jpeg)

A category like pharma, with its massive piles of powerful consumer data, and the need to deploy that in a privacy-first way, would benefit tremendously from more automation.

“I think it’s happening. I think it’s happening more and more. And I think it’s not going to be unique to TV,” said Rosen. “I do think outcomes are going to more and more often become the key metric…and There is insight [needed] to be continuously optimizing.”

Yet at the same time, Rosen points out how careful brands must be if and when they enter this space. And there needs to be a clear payoff.

Brands have to “ensure that the data inputs that are going into those AI approaches are rock solid,” said Rosen. “Because I think what the fear would be is that if you AI is not gonna fix a weak signal. It’s gonna make whatever’s underneath move faster, so you think you’re getting to a better outcome. But if that input right off the bat was weak, you risk getting into trouble.”

“I call that the doom loop of AI, right? The way to avoid that is to ensure you have the best quality, scaled, first-party data inputs from the start.”

That is assuming of course, that the TV advertising system will allow you to make the best use of such data inputs. Are we anywhere close to that?

Check out the full episode here:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0-7ZWiaYfT8)

### Dive Brief:

*   More U.S. households feel financially vulnerable – 17% compared to 15% in 2025 – reversing progress recorded a year ago, according to a [survey from The Financial Health Network](https://finhealthnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Financial-Health-Pulse-2026-U.S.-Trends-Report-Mounting-Pressure-Growing-Vulnerability.pdf) and the University of Southern California.
*   Less than 70% said they paid all their bills on time over the past 12 months, down 3 points from last year, per the research. Those reporting “unmanageable levels of debt” rose from 29% to 31%.
*   Since 2019, low-income consumers shifted more than $10 billion from discretionary purchases toward essentials like groceries, while higher-income consumers shifted more than twice that amount toward discretionary spending, according to research from Numerator.

### Dive Insight:

Pandemic-era financial support from the federal government has dried up and inflation is taking a toll, leaving more U.S. households struggling, according to this research from The Financial Health Network and the University of Southern California’s Dornsife Center for Economic and Social Research.

For many, the future also looks bleak, as the number of consumers expecting to be worse off financially in five years “rose sharply between 2020 and 2026,” according to their report.

This is hitting certain populations especially hard.

Recently enacted restrictions on federal nutrition and medical assistance programs have offset tax breaks. Student loan delinquencies — a [priority during the Biden administration](https://www.retaildive.com/news/student-debt-relief-holiday-retail-impact/688630/)— are now occurring at high rates, with more than a quarter of student loan borrowers saying they are financially vulnerable, up from 21% last year.Many immigrants have left the workforce amid [heightened immigration enforcement](https://www.retaildive.com/news/how-the-retail-crime-bill-could-bolster-ice/829731/), which has reduced spending in that cohort.

Since January 2018, prices have risen 35% for low-income consumers and 31% for high-income consumers, according to Numerator.

“Perhaps in response to the volatility of the post-pandemic world, U.S. households began to express a growing sense of financial uncertainty and pessimism,” the Financial Health Network authors said in their report. “Uncertainty about expectations for both earnings growth and inflation grew following the pandemic.”

Despite these pressures, consumer spending has [held steady this year](https://www.retaildive.com/news/monthly-retail-sales-from-the-us-commerce-department/574252/) even on discretionary items.

“That said, macro pressures have persisted and intensified, elevated inflation, higher oil prices, and other disruptions could weigh on consumers more than expected so far, pressuring sales trends in 2026 with additional challenges such as increasing transit costs and other commodity prices,” Telsey Advisory Group analysts led by Dana Telsey said in a Tuesday research note.

Retail sales in the segments covered by Retail Dive rose 6.7% year over year in August, buoyed somewhat by later-than-usual shopping for back to school, according to Chip West,retail and consumer behavior expert at RRD. Strong spending should continue into this month and next “as consumers keep finding ways to spend and retailers move aggressively to get holiday inventory in front of shoppers earlier,” he said in emailed comments last week.

“Many consumers are tapping into their savings to continue spending, but how long that can continue will depend in part on where gas prices go from here,” he said.
