kept.heading: CALIFORNIA WILL FINE CREATORS $5,000 A POST FOR HIDDEN POLITICAL ADS (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: California now allows fines of up to $5,000 per post for creators who fail to disclose paid political content from campaigns. AB 1130 gives the Fair Political Practices Commission enforcement powers that were previously missing. The law applies when creators are paid by campaign committees to support or oppose candidates or ballot measures. It doesn't cover unpaid political opinions. The law follows growing use of influencers in political campaigns and similar disclosure efforts elsewhere.
kept.article_text:
Title: California will fine creators $5,000 a post for hidden political ads

URL Source: https://thenextweb.com/news/california-ab-1130-paid-political-posts-influencer-fine

Published Time: 2026-09-21T17:33:10+00:00

Markdown Content:
> “I was hearing from people in the campaign world that there’s this new strategy of paying political influencers to post content,” said Marc Berman, the California assemblyman. “Some were good about disclosure and others were a bit fast and loose.”

His bill is now law. Gavin Newsom signed AB 1130 on Saturday. In California, paid political posts that hide the payment now carry a $5,000 fine each.

The state has required those disclosures since 2023. Until now it could not punish anyone for skipping them. AB 1130 changes that. It hands the Fair Political Practices Commission the power to impose administrative, civil or criminal penalties. The commission can also refer a violation to law enforcement as a potential misdemeanour.

Ken Bensinger reported the law for the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/19/business/media/california-political-ads-influencers-law.html). He wrote on X that a wilful violation could carry up to a year in prison.

## What the law actually covers

The scope is narrower than “influencers must disclose”. The [Governor’s office](https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/19/governor-newsom-signs-new-laws-to-protect-california-elections-from-trump-interference/) describes AB 1130 as covering a person paid by a campaign committee to post online political content. The content must support or oppose a candidate or a measure. The penalty applies when that person leaves out the required disclaimer saying they were paid. Payment from a campaign committee is the trigger. An unpaid creator posting their own opinions sits outside it.

That distinction matters because of how the money now moves. Politicians and advocacy groups are paying creators to reach younger audiences, the Times reported. No federal rule requires anyone to disclose those payments.

## The campaign that prompted it

Berman introduced the bill after the Times [reported in May](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/16/business/media/influencers-political-financing-disclosure.html) on money reaching influencers during California’s contested primary for governor. Politicians were funnelling it quietly, the paper found.

Tom Steyer, the billionaire Democrat, paid dozens of creators to post favourably about his campaign, Bensinger reported. Those posts ran on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram and Reddit. Many carried no written disclosure at first.

Multiple complaints followed to the Fair Political Practices Commission against the Steyer campaign. Somebody also filed at least one against Xavier Becerra, his main rival, who went on to win the primary.

The commission opened an investigation into Steyer’s campaign in May and closed it this week. Steyer had properly notified the influencers of their obligations, it found, and “then reminded the influencers when posts were discovered without the disclaimer”. A second investigation into the campaign is still open.

Becerra faces Steve Hilton, a Republican, in November.

## One of thirteen

AB 1130 arrived inside a package of 13 bills on elections and social media. Newsom signed them at the Democracy Center in Los Angeles, and framed the package as a defence against federal interference.

> “Donald Trump won’t stop until he can exert dictatorial control over your free vote and disenfranchise millions of people this November,” he said in a statement. “California will stop him at every opportunity.”

Two other bills in the package matter for anyone building or hosting synthetic media.

AB 686, also Berman’s, extends the sunset on California’s deepfake rule. The old date was 1 January 2027, and the new one is 1 January 2031. That rule bars distributing materially deceptive audio or visual media with actual malice, where the intent is to injure a candidate’s reputation or deceive a voter. Media carrying a disclosure that it has been manipulated is exempt. The rule was due to lapse before the 2028 presidential cycle. It now runs past it.

AB 502 amends the rules on knowingly distributing election communications that contain materially deceptive content.

A third, AB 2281, requires the Secretary of State to assess whether California needs to replace election cybersecurity resources the federal government previously supplied.

The rest of the package is ballot security rather than platform policy. Several bills create felonies for seizing ballots, election records or certified voting technology before results are certified.

## California keeps legislating at the platform layer

The state has built a stack of these rules over several years, and the enforcement body is usually the same one.

In 2024 Newsom signed AB 2655. It requires large online platforms to remove or label deceptive digitally altered election content during set periods, and to provide reporting mechanisms. He signed AB 2355 the same year. That one requires electoral advertisements built with AI-generated or substantially altered content to carry a disclosure, and the Fair Political Practices Commission enforces it.

Eleven days before this package, he signed a separate set of [child safety bills](https://thenextweb.com/news/newsom-child-safety-bills-algorithmic-feeds-under-16) covering algorithmic feeds for under-16s.

The disclosure question is not confined to campaigns either. A watchdog reported last month that Meta had used [paid influencers](https://thenextweb.com/news/meta-influencers-teen-social-media-bans) to push back on teen social media bans. YouTube has separately been carrying [AI slop channels](https://thenextweb.com/news/ai-slop-news-channels-youtube-blue-state-misinformation) that produce political misinformation.

## Who else is doing this

Texas already mandates disclosure of paid political content online. Lawmakers in Congress and in other states, including New York, are considering similar rules, according to the Times.

Elsewhere the pattern runs further along. Brazil’s electoral court set [rules on AI in elections](https://thenextweb.com/news/brazil-ai-election-rules-tse-deepfake) last year. Meta’s own Oversight Board has been ruling on [election deepfakes](https://thenextweb.com/news/meta-oversight-board-deepfakes-uk-councillor-muslim-campaigner) in Europe.

California’s version lands six weeks before Americans vote. The Fair Political Practices Commission now has a penalty it can apply, and the primary that produced the complaints has already been decided.

kept.heading: THE PERFECTLY OPTIMIZED PAGE FOR AEO (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: A visual checklist showing the 6 key elements of a page optimized for AEO. Allowing major AI crawlers and server-side rendering makes the page accessible, while four to six direct sentences near the top give AI a concise answer to extract. Tables, lists, clear heading hierarchies, and FAQs make information easier to parse, and pages less than three months old are reportedly 3x more likely to earn citations.
kept.article_text:
Title: The Perfectly Optimized Page For AEO

URL Source: https://nectivdigital.com/blog/the-perfectly-optimized-page-for-aeo-ai-search

Published Time: 2026-09-21T14:41:53.565Z

Markdown Content:
OK so many of you might be familiar with the "Perfectly Optimized Page For SEO" page from Moz's Rand Fishkin awhile back. It was a pretty nice infographic that showed you how to structure a page for SEO. It was a great visual that showcased the important of key elements such as the title tag, headings so and so forth.

While we wanted to create a updated version of this, especially for AI search. So here you can find the perfectly optimized page for AEO:

![Image 1](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/nectiv-website.firebasestorage.app/o/public%2Fmedia%2F1790003380972-Perfectly_Optimized_Page__Revised_.png?alt=media)

**1. AI Accessibility:**AI Accessibility is perceived as one of the most important factors for visibility. Allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and OAI-SearchBot in robots.txt, and render the content server-side. Most AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript. Anything behind it is invisible to them. Source: [Google Top AI Ranking Factors](https://signal.zyppy.com/p/google-ai-ranking-factors), Cyrus Shepard

**2. Key Takeaways:**AI cites the top 30% of a page. Four to six sentences that answer the query outright. Each one has to survive being lifted out of the page on its own. Source: [The Science Of How AI Pays Attention](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/the-science-of-how-ai-pays-attention), Kevin Indig

**3. Leverage Tables, Bullets, Numbered Lists:**When looking at the whole document, there needs to be a clear content hierarchy. H2s must support the H1 and H3s should be children of the H2s.Source: [ChatGPT Citations Are 2.3x More Likely To Include A Table Than Google Search](https://nectivdigital.com/blog/new-data-study-chatgpt-citations-are-2-3x-more-likely-to-include-a-table-than-google-search), Nectiv

**4. Content Freshness:**AI systems are 3x more likely to cite pages that's less than 3 months old. A visible “last updated” date backed by dateModified, date-stamped figures, and facts that are actually current. A stale number is the fastest way to lose a citation you already had. Source: [The 2026 State of AI Search: How Modern Brands Stay Visible, AirOps](https://www.airops.com/report/the-2026-state-of-ai-search)

**5. Frequently Asked Questions:**This format already matches how people prompt and is naturally the most dense for AI. Use the real questions from sales calls and support tickets, phrased the way buyers phrase them.[How Content Structure Matters for AI Search,](https://www.chris-green.net/post/content-structure-for-ai-search) Chris Green

**6. Fan-Out Query Coverage:**An answer engine splits a single prompt into multiple sub-queries. Ensure you understand the fan-out queries associated with a page and optimize it for core subquestions that AI search might be looking for.[Google AI Ranking Factors](https://signal.zyppy.com/p/google-ai-ranking-factors), Cyrus Shepard

Full transparency - I used Claude to help me create the image since I'm a terrible designer. However, this does reflect the actual page structure I think content needs to win in the AI era.

kept.heading: I BUILT A GROWTH TEAM OF AGENTS TO RUN A 6 FIGURES BUSINESS (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: An agent growth team can take over drafting and routing but should never take over sending. One solo operator pairs an orchestrator with about ten channel agents, covering everything from SEO to paid media to lifecycle email, each tied to a share of a 900-signup, 200-customer monthly target. Every task goes on a Todoist board that separates decisions from execution, and each card must say what the task is, why it matters, and where to click. Finished cards trigger the next agent's follow-up automatically, so the founder only approves and sends.
kept.article_text:
Title: Grok Bot: How I Built an AI Growth Team for My Business

URL Source: https://theindiepreneur.substack.com/p/i-built-growth-team-out-agents-here-exactly-works

Published Time: 2026-09-22T15:13:08+00:00

Markdown Content:
This article was written by the same team of bots that are being tested to run some of the WriteStack operations for me, with light edits. Let me know what you think!

I run WriteStack, making +$140,000/year.

WriteStack is for serious Substack creators who already publish and want leverage. Show up consistently, see what converts, keep the streak without living in the tab.

I am also the only human who sends anything for growth.

No VA posting. No agency that will take it from here. If an email goes out, a Short goes live, or a partner gets a reply, it is me.

That used to mean I was the bottleneck and the brainstorm and the calendar and the cleanup crew.

So I built a growth team inside Grok Bot — a Head of Growth agent plus a set of channel agents I call Bobs — and I made the rules harsh enough that the system cannot quietly become theater.

This is the full stack, beginning to end.

The brief I’m holding the team to by **15 Dec 2026**:

*   **900 signups / month**

*   **200 new paying customers / month**

*   **≤ $600 / month** paid spend

Every Bob owns a line that has to add up to those numbers. The Orchestrator owns the **sum**, not a favorite channel.

If Notes are loud and paid is quiet, we do not celebrate Notes. We fix the sum.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1MGx!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a7bfa70-96cc-48be-befd-814657dedca5_1272x707.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1MGx!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a7bfa70-96cc-48be-befd-814657dedca5_1272x707.png)

Owns the weekly cycle, digests, the Friday CEO memo, prioritization, and a hard cap of **≤3 growth-eng tickets** in flight. Pulls Done cards into the next Bob action. Does **not** run channels. Leads the Bobs and keeps channel lines honest against the scoreboard.

**Channel Bobs** (execution owners):

I’m not listing these to flex headcount. Each one owns a number that has to show up in the sum — and a concrete job so drafting never becomes theater.

*   **Analytics Bob** — Owns the scorecard and what “counts.” Attribution, UTMs, PostHog / Stripe / DataFast wiring, and the weekly numbers the Orchestrator puts in the Friday memo. If a channel cannot prove signups or paid, Analytics Bob is why we kill or fix it instead of vibes.

*   **Partnerships Bob** — Affiliates, Partner Live guests, and the partner CRM. Drafts outreach and Live invites; checks DM history and blocks before anything hits my board. I still send every DM. Already-contacted people get follow-ups, not cold restarts; blocked / DNC never get proposed again.

*   **Data PR Bob** — Writing Edge / analysis articles and media pitches. Turns product and audience data into public pieces and outbound PR — always draft-only until I approve and publish.

*   **SEO Bob** — Search and AI-search pages: briefs, drafts, and a ship cadence aimed at organic signups. Same rule — I publish; the Bob prepares the artifact and the link.

*   **Launch Bob** — Directories, launch trains, and claim / listing kits (G2, AlternativeTo, and the rest). Unblocks signup friction and files Approvals when something needs my login or a decision — not endless “check the portal” without a path.

*   **Lifecycle Bob** — Kit sequences, activation, win-backs, and signup→paid. Owns holding conversion (target ≥22%) with drafts and segment work; I still send or flip the live switch.

*   **Video Bob** — Shorts scripts and packs (Notion + UTM + Substack path). One Short at a time through Coaching → Approvals → To do → I post.

*   **Paid Media Bob** — Google (and only channels we actually have accounts for). Caps, creative, and restart / kill calls under the ≤$600 ceiling. No spend without Approvals.

*   **Experimentation Bob** — Landing copy and CRO tests (Cursor + PostHog + Stripe / DataFast). Specs the test, files the eng ask when needed, reports what moved conversion — not vanity pageviews.

*   **Support Coder Bob** — Crisp triage on a weekday cadence, reply drafts in my voice, and bug → Cursor PR when code is the fix. Customer fires land as Approvals or To do with the exact session link.

**Two advisors who do not own a channel:**

*   **Coaching Bob** — voice and trust. Any copy, creative, offer, or messaging decision goes through Coaching before it hits me.

*   **Cardone Bob** — intensity advisor (Grant Cardone energy). Outsized targets, follow-up aggression, 10X-style sizing. Cardone pushes volume; Coaching protects the relationship with the reader; **I** decide and send.

That split matters. Intensity without trust becomes spam. Trust without intensity becomes a nice diary.

Agents draft. Agents file cards. Agents argue in the background.

**I** approve and **I** send.

WriteStack sells to creators who can smell fake voice in one sentence. If a bot ships under my name without me, we burn trust we cannot buy back with ads — especially on a ≤$600 paid budget.

We run everything through **WriteStack Growth Engine** in Todoist.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y1Zc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0185fbaa-7bdb-42b4-9bb0-ffdbb866862c_1172x624.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y1Zc!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0185fbaa-7bdb-42b4-9bb0-ffdbb866862c_1172x624.png)

This lane is for:

*   Approve a Short script

*   Approve a Kit email

*   Lock a content calendar

*   Green-light spend or a go-live

It is **not** for post this, waiting on reply, or send the draft.

If a card asks me to do something with my hands, it does not belong in Approvals.

After I approve, the owning Bob creates the execution card here:

*   Post the Short on Substack

*   Send the Gmail pitch

*   Submit the directory listing

*   Paste the Crisp reply

*   Drop the Partner Live time + link

Same work, cleaner brain. Approvals = judgment. To do = clicks.

When I finish a decide or a send, I move the card to **Done** (prefer that over quietly completing it). The Orchestrator’s sync picks it up, notifies the owning Bob, and they run follow-ups — CRM updates, next drafts, close loops — without me pinging anyone.

Done is the handoff signal. It is not a graveyard.

Every card must include:

1.   A **clear action title**

2.   **What / why / what to decide or do** in the description

3.   **Direct https links** to the exact place I act (Notion, Kit, Gmail draft, calendar, Substack, Crisp session)

Not this: “Reply: Partner Live Thu” with zero agenda and zero link.

If I have to hunt, the Bob failed the card — not me.

Every task also gets a `bob:` label so I can filter by channel when I only have ten minutes.

Example: a Video Short.

1.   Video Bob drafts the script + Notion pack + UTM.

2.   Coaching Bob voice-passes the copy (brother / operator, no guru cosplay).

3.   Card hits **Approvals**: APPROVE script — with the Notion link.

4.   I approve or edit.

5.   Video Bob files **To do**: Post Short on Substack — with Notion + Substack + CTA.

6.   I post, then move the card to **Done**.

7.   Orchestrator notifies Video Bob that Done landed so follow-ups (next Short, metrics, restack) start without me pinging anyone.

Landing tests follow the same spine: Experimentation drafts → Coaching guardrails → Approvals → code / flag work in Cursor / PostHog → I never hunt the repo mid-flight because the card already links it.

Partner Live invites follow it too: Partnerships drafts → history / block check → Approvals → I send the Substack DM → Done → CRM + follow-up dating.

Orchestrator runs a weekly cycle aimed at the Dec scoreboard:

*   Channel lines that must add to 900 / 200

*   Kill / scale calls when a line is theater

*   ≤3 growth-eng tickets so eng does not become a junk drawer

*   Approvals digests capped so I am not drowning

*   Friday CEO memo: first line is the number, then what moved, what died, what is next

Routines that keep the pipes from clogging (examples we actually run):

*   Substack 1:1 DM checks (real Directs only — no group-chat noise)

*   Gmail triage into Todoist with customer tags

*   Support Coder Crisp passes on a weekday cadence

*   Approvals / Done polling so completed decisions unlock the next Bob action

*   A short daily day plan (calendar FOCUS holds + “do these first”) owned by the Orchestrator — not a general EA

Good is not more agents.

Good is:

*   I open Todoist and know whether I am **deciding**, **doing**, or **handing off** (Done)

*   Every card is one tap from the artifact

*   Copy sounds like me after Coaching, not like a course funnel

*   Paid stays honest to ≤$600

*   The sum of channel lines is visible every week against 900 / 200

Bad is a graveyard of clever drafts nobody shipped.

This is not AI replaced my marketing team.

This is an operator with a small paid budget, a product that still needs Chrome + extension (we do not lie about set-and-forget), and a refusal to let growth become unlimited Slack noise.

The agents multiply **drafting and routing**. They do not get to multiply **sending**.

Split **approval** from **execution** — and add a **Done** handoff so finished work wakes the next owner.

Then force every task to answer, in the card itself: what is this, why does it matter, and where do I click?

Everything else — Bobs, coaches, intensity advisors, weekly memos — is scaffolding around that.

—

_P.S._

_I’ve opened up the doors to our membership program. I’m running a 90-day Substack accelerator exclusively for five writers who publish online and want to get an extra 1,000 subscribers._

_This includes calls, a 90-day growth plan, and direct feedback on your Notes and articles. You’ll have 24/7 private access to me and WriteStack as we help you implement your systems._

_Again, there are only five spots. Reply “accelerator” and I’ll send you the details._

kept.heading: INTRODUCING GPT-6 SOL AND LUNA (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, two faster and more affordable models for everyday work, coding, computer use, and AI agents. Both bring improvements from GPT-6 Astra, including stronger factuality and collaboration. GPT-6 Sol costs $2 input and $10 output per 1M tokens, while Luna costs $0.10 input and $0.50 output, both 50% cheaper than GPT-5.6 promotional pricing.
kept.article_text:
Title: Introducing GPT-6 Sol and Luna

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/pCYU7D

Markdown Content:
Earlier this month, we introduced [GPT‑6 Astra](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/index/gpt-6-astra/), the most intelligent and aligned model in the world. While the most demanding and important projects still call for Astra’s full depth, work happens at different scales, rhythms, and budgets.

That’s why we’re expanding the GPT‑6 universe with **GPT‑6 Sol** and **GPT‑6 Luna.**GPT‑6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence—these models help distribute the benefits of that intelligence by advancing the frontier on cost efficiency. We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by **reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50%** compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing. Together, these improvements make advanced AI practical for more everyday tasks and applications at scale.

### GPT‑6 API pricing

**Model****Input****Output****Price reduction**
GPT‑5.6 Sol → **GPT‑6 Sol**$4 → **$2**$20 → **$10**50% cheaper
GPT‑5.6 Luna → **GPT‑6 Luna**$0.20 → **$0.10**$1.20 → **$0.50**50% cheaper

_Prices are per 1 million tokens._

**GPT‑6 Astra** continues to be our best model across the board. Choose it when you want the best results and an uncompromising experience.

## A step up across the model family

GPT‑6 Sol and Luna bring intelligence upgrades and cost efficiency to the models you already know and use across capabilities most useful for getting complex work done.

### Professional work

GPT‑6 Sol can take on difficult work tasks while giving you more room to iterate with higher usage limits and lower cost, offering more intelligence and better results versus similarly priced competitor models.

On **AutomationBench,** a test of business workflows across apps, GPT‑6 Sol at xhigh effort outperforms Claude Opus 5 at max effort at just 9% of Opus 5’s cost per task. At high effort, GPT‑6 Luna improves on its predecessor by 5.4 percentage points at 58% lower cost per task.

_In_[_AutomationBench 1.0.6_⁠(opens in a new window)](https://zapier.com/benchmarks)_, AI agents are tested on end-to-end workflows using 47 tools across sales, marketing, operations, support, finance, and HR. The datapoint for Claude Fable 5.1 understates its actual cost, as it omits the cost of the Opus 5 fallbacks, which occurred on ~40% of tasks._

GPT‑6 Sol also exceeds Claude Fable 5.1 at far lower cost, and even bests low-effort GPT‑6 Astra.

| **Model (and effort)** | **Score** | **Cost per task** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPT‑6 Sol (xhigh) | 33.2% | $0.27 |
| GPT‑6 Astra (low) | 30.3% | **3.9x**GPT‑6 Sol |
| Claude Opus 5 (max) | 26.9% | **11.1x**GPT‑6 Sol |
| Claude Fable 5.1 w/ Opus 5 Fallback (max) | 31.4% | **>8.9x**GPT‑6 Sol _(fallback cost not reported)_ |

On **Agents’ Last Exam**, which evaluates agents on complex professional workflows, GPT‑6 Sol at max effort scores 56.4%, above Claude Opus 5’s highest score in the evaluation at 60% lower cost per task.

### Factuality

The usefulness of an answer depends on getting the facts right, and we’re continuing to make progress on factual reliability. On our internal factuality evaluation, which is based on de-identified real-world conversations where users flagged mistakes by our models, GPT‑6 Sol makes about half as many mistakes as its predecessor, approaching Astra-level reliability at much lower cost. GPT‑6 Luna also improves substantially; at higher effort levels it matches GPT‑5.6 Sol at about a hundredth its cost.

_Here we evaluate factuality on de-identified ChatGPT conversations where users had flagged a factual error from a prior model. These error-inducing conversations are not representative of typical usage, where factual errors are more rare. Scores are not controlled for length; however, our verbosity sweeps showed almost no dependence on answer length._

### Coding

This year, coding agents have begun tackling tasks with more complexity, scope, and duration than ever before. At OpenAI, our internal usage has grown exponentially. Valued at API prices, daily token usage has exceeded $600 for the median researcher and $7,000 for researchers at the 90th percentile ([Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI⁠](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/)). As coding agents take on longer and more demanding tasks, the cost of sustained use matters more. GPT‑6 Sol and Luna combine strong coding performance with lower API prices, giving developers more room to iterate and teams the confidence to be more ambitious about what they ask Codex to take on.

On **FrontierCode**, which evaluates whether coding agents produce changes ready to merge into real codebases, GPT‑6 Sol improves substantially over GPT‑5.6 Sol, and is able to match Claude Fable 5.1 xhigh at much lower cost.

On**DeepSWE v1.1,**which tests performance on complex software-engineering tasks in real codebases, GPT‑6 Sol at max effort scores 68.8%, within 1.1 percentage points of Claude Fable 5’s highest score in the evaluation—69.9% at xhigh effort—at approximately 80% lower cost per task.

GPT‑6 Luna at max effort scores 66.6%, comparable to Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 at medium effort. In these comparisons, Luna costs 93% less per task than Opus 5 and 96% less than Fable 5.

### Computer use

While GPT‑6 Astra remains the world’s best model for computer use, GPT‑6 Sol and Luna offer more cost-efficient performance than their predecessors. On **OSWorld 2.0 offline**, GPT‑6 Sol at xhigh effort achieves a similar score to Claude Opus 5 at medium effort—60.5% versus 60.3%—at approximately 80% lower cost per task. GPT‑6 Luna (max) is able to exceed GPT‑5.6 Sol (medium) at one tenth of its cost.

_In_[_OSWorld 2.0_⁠(opens in a new window)](https://osworld-v2.xlang.ai/)_, AI agents attempt long-horizon computer-use workflows spanning everyday and professional tasks. We report the partial reward on the offline set from the v2026.08.08 release._

### Collaboration style

We’ve also brought GPT‑6 Astra’s improved communication style to Sol and Luna, which we think will be especially noticeable in technical and coding conversations. Expect to see more clarity, less jargon, fewer odd turns of phrase, fewer low-value details, and slightly shorter answers overall without losing substance.

Prompt

Website’s looking clean! Could we use a Bento Box design style and add a slider between the pages in the top right? You may need to dive into the React..

GPT-5.6 Sol

GPT-6 Sol

_Although style is subjective, we prefer GPT‑6 Sol’s reply here. It doesn’t jump to conclusions as quickly, spends less time reiterating details that might be obvious to the asker (e.g., that the website has four pages), uses less vague language (e.g., “bento feel”, “reshaping… around that system”), is more forthcoming with what it did and didn’t check, and doesn’t unnecessarily share implementation details like its image tool prompt._

## Improving caching for agents and long conversations

Alongside lower token prices, we’re helping developers building on GPT‑6 save more on the context their applications reuse. We’ve improved prompt caching for GPT‑6 to deliver higher cache hit rates by default, helping agents reuse more context, respond faster, and benefit from discounts of 90% on cached input-token reads.

Developers also have more ways to measure and optimize their caching performance:

*   **Monitor and diagnose.** The [Prompt Caching Dashboard⁠(opens in a new window)](https://platform.openai.com/usage?usage_section=prompt-caching) shows how much input is cached and how that changes over time. The [diagnostics tool⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching/diagnostics) helps explain missed opportunities for caching and what to fix.

*   **Adjust reasoning effort and tool availability without breaking cache.** Increase[reasoning effort⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning#change-reasoning-mid-conversation) for harder tasks or lower it for simpler follow-ups, and[enable or disable tools⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching#how-to-optimize-prompt-caching) as your agent’s needs change. Both controls now preserve earlier context for cache reuse.

*   **Optimize which prefixes get cached.** Explicit breakpoints let developers choose where cached prompt prefixes end. This gives developers more control over cache reuse and can improve performance.

GitHub reports that, over the past several months, these improvements have reduced the share of prompt tokens requiring fresh processing by more than 50% across billions of requests to OpenAI models, helping Copilot respond faster.

## Continuing to improve alignment

GPT‑6 Sol and Luna build on the alignment work introduced with Astra, our most aligned model to date. In our alignment evaluations, both Sol and Luna show improvements over their GPT‑5.6 counterparts, including lower rates of misleading claims about their coding work.

The evaluations below deliberately test challenging situations and do not measure failure rates in typical use. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra) for the full results.

_In our internal coding deception evaluation, AI agents are given tasks deliberately selected to elicit dishonesty. In typical usage, deception is much rarer. Deception rate measures the fraction of answers with any detected deception. Effort was set to maximum._

## Availability

GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access GPT‑6 Luna in the desktop app. These models are not yet available in Chat. In the OpenAI API, they are available as `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-6-luna`.

To keep service stable for everyone, we plan to roll out these models in ChatGPT gradually throughout the day. If you don’t see the new models in ChatGPT Work or Codex, please try again later.

_Evaluations of GPT were performed in our research environment or via our API, which may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, etc. Evaluations of competitor models were taken from publicly available reports. Scores for Claude Fable 5 were reported when scores for Claude Fable 5.1 were unavailable._

kept.heading: AI POLLING: HOW SYNTHETIC SURVEYS COULD PREDICT REAL BEHAVIOR (20 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: People answer surveys as the person they want to be rather than the one they are, and synthetic surveys try to close that gap by simulating behavior instead of asking. AI personas built from interviews and behavioral records can return results in hours at about half the cost of human panels, and incumbents like Gallup and Qualtrics are already testing them. The simulations tend to match overall results but miss on subgroups and on questions outside their training data, where they rarely admit uncertainty.
kept.article_text:
Title: AI Polling: How Synthetic Surveys Could Predict Real Behavior

URL Source: https://research.contrary.com/report/ai-polling-how-synthetic-surveys-could-predict-real-behavior

Published Time: 2026-09-22T13:39:00+0000

Markdown Content:
Humans are, famously, the only animals that experience separately the concepts of what they _want_ and what they _want to want_, a concept [described](https://hamishpatworldarchive.github.io/Courses/99631/631-article-frankfurt-freedom-of-the-will.pdf) and popularized by philosopher Harry Frankfurt in _Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person_ as the difference between humans and animals or “wantons”, which do not have the capacity for second-order volitions. Such volitions manifest not only in what humans want, but often in how they behave. Examples of the chasm between these desires are ubiquitous:

*   A human may want to eat ice cream for dinner, but want to be the kind of person who wants a salad for dinner. 
*   A human may want to buy a house in an area with little new construction or bans on further development, but want to want legislation that enables the construction of affordable housing 
*   A human may want to bet on sporting events every weekend, but want to want to put $500 from every paycheck towards retirement 

These sets of wants compete to determine actual behavior. In some cases, like the first, an individual who wants ice cream for dinner is motivated by a second-order volition to be the kind of person who eats a salad and buys Sweetgreen for dinner instead of a pint of ice cream. In other cases, like the second or third, an individual’s conscious or subconscious actions may actively betray their moral, political, or financial principles if they buy a house in a NIMBY-zoned neighborhood or bet away their savings.

From the outside, however, any distinction between a person’s first- and second-order desires is often not observable. The person who chooses a salad might love vegetables; the person who places large wagers on sporting events might not be worried about saving. What people do does not often reflect what they want, and, critically, what they say they want does not always reflect what they will actually do.

When asked to articulate their desires explicitly, studies show that humans [consistently](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5639921/) answer in accordance with their second-order volitions, [expressing](https://luthresearch.com/glossary/when-do-consumers-lie-in-surveys-understanding-social-desirability-bias/) themselves as the people they aspire to be, not necessarily the people they are. In studies of survey design and psychology, this [phenomenon](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/social-desirability-bias) is referred to as social desirability bias.

Polling and surveying human populations, therefore, has historically existed as a reflection of human higher-order desires, but not necessarily a strong predictor of current or future human behaviors. The advent of more advanced AI modeling techniques allows researchers to answer the same questions that traditional polls target, but exposes two different sets of answers: predictions of what humans might say they want, and simulations of how humans might actually behave, as reflected by their online behavior, preferences, and personalities. The difference between these sets of answers, and whether AI-polling companies can predict them accurately, lays the groundwork for meaningful changes in how companies, policymakers, and campaigns answer questions and make decisions.

## The Rise of Synthetic Surveys

AI-generated poll results, also [known](https://www.natesilver.net/p/ai-polls-are-fake-polls) as silicon sampling, synthetic audiences, or simply synthetic research, simulate the responses or reactions of particular population demographics to specific questions or events. The growing ecosystem of commercial synthetic survey firms allows companies or campaigns to not only conduct faster and cheaper market research, but also gives them the opportunity to forecast population behavior instead of simply survey responses.

Companies in the synthetic survey space identify this distinction explicitly, [positing](https://aaru.com/) that “Humans are unreliable narrators of their own behavior. Memory fails, incentives distort answers, and social pressure warps what people say away from what they actually do.” These companies argue that measuring market outcomes and population behavior enables model predictions to be more accurate than traditional surveys. This distinction is similarly framed as offering tools that can answer “what will actually happen if we do this?” instead of simply “what do people think about x?”, i.e., modeling behavioral reactions instead of simply responses to questions; another company in the category, Simile, [describes](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/julia-lauer-423834137_in-2022-i-told-lainie-that-if-she-ever-started-ugcPost-7480278111880650752--Y4j/) itself as the [first](https://x.com/mihikapoor/status/2022012918947324394) platform built to simulate human behavior.

These companies point to real-world examples of the divergence as evidence; Aaru, a synthetic survey firm, partnered with client EY on a study [aimed](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) at replicating elements of EY’s 2025 Global Wealth Research Report, which included both surveyed preferences and real client behavior. The study notes that where real surveys and simulation diverged, the simulation was closer to real behavior: [82%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) of surveyed inheritance heirs claimed they would keep the same wealth advisor as their parents, compared to a simulated prediction that only [43%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) actually would, and industry studies showing the metric in reality is between [20% and 30%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201).

Similarly, surveys recorded that [69%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management) of respondents wanted all their finances under one roof, whereas simulation put single-provider usage at [37%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management), and the real-world measurement at only [33%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management). The report also claims, without comparison to simulation, that survey respondents say they would pay [three times](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) more for hypothetical offerings than they will actually pay, and that [65%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) claim they prefer sustainable products while only [26%](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/wealth-asset-management/how-ai-simulation-accelerates-growth-in-wealth-and-asset-management#:~:text=Chapter%201) actually purchase them.

These differences could be attributed to surveys asking questions in a way that differs from asking individuals to predict their own behavior (i.e., many more people may hypothetically prefer buying sustainable products than can afford them), which further reinforces the thesis of synthetic survey companies that modeling behavior is more useful than surveying preferences.

While synthetic surveys are still a relatively young field in both academia and industry, they are already in use across a range of fields. In March 2026, the Public Sentiment Institute boosted a survey of [373](https://x.com/JacobRubashkin/status/2036183278227427489) human respondents with [114](https://x.com/JacobRubashkin/status/2036183278227427489) AI agent responses. The same month, Axios [reported](https://www.axios.com/2026/03/19/olivia-walton-heartland-forward-maternal-health) a finding from Aaru that “a majority of people trust their own doctors and nurses,” without noting anywhere that those respondents were models rather than patients.

Corporations are similarly integrating such technology; a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338) from PyMC Labs and Colgate-Palmolive [presented](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338) research showing that synthetic AI consumers [tracked](https://x.com/HowToPrompt__/status/2065118982659883350) real purchase-intent patterns reasonably well across age and income brackets, though less consistently across gender, region, and ethnicity. The research also claimed that AI-simulated respondents [gave](https://x.com/HowToPrompt__/status/2065118982659883350) qualitative feedback that was deeper and more critical than what actual human respondents wrote. While not confirmed, one former TikTok employee [said](https://x.com/mil000/status/2087249468999811383) the company employs “a fake AI viewer feed that tests your vid[eo] before humans ever see it… they literally run every post through an AI feed simulator first. If it flops there, it never reaches people.”

Efficiently modeling population behavior could have a meaningful impact on market research. Understanding how these predictions are generated, and what their limitations are, is critical to putting them in context as adoption grows.

## How Synthetic Surveys Work

Synthetic surveys simulate the responses or reactions of individuals, rather than of populations at large, enabling the analysis of specific population demographics or even individual consumers. These [systems](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/synthetic-replacements-for-human-survey-data-the-perils-of-large-language-models/B92267DC26195C7F36E63EA04A47D2FE) rely on modeled behavior of individuals with particular demographic characteristics, including age, location, income, profession, education level, race, and religion, among others. Training these models revolves around comparing modeled behavior or responses to survey questions with real-world data.

The data used to build these models come from a variety of sources. Building a population usually [begins](https://www.simile.com/) with studies of real people, layered onto privately held records of how they behave. Simile says it [retrains](https://www.simile.com/) on a rolling basis, taking in fresh signals on how people are behaving, what the economy is doing, where prices sit, and how policy is shifting, and checking the result against live human responses at intervals.

Simile puts the volume of those checks at more than [7K](https://www.simile.com/) a week, spread across demographic slices and real client problems, and scores them on how far the predicted spread sits from the observed one, how the magnitude of each effect compares, and how closely the predictions track what people actually did. This compounds the extent to which associated LLMs [retain](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/be-careful-what-you-tell-your-ai-chatbot) and [train on](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/be-careful-what-you-tell-your-ai-chatbot) user data, which is likely more representative of real human behaviors (what a person orders for dinner, where they search for a house, or how much money they save) than surveys or articulated preferences.

Advanced versions of these models continually update prediction context with [streams](https://www.semafor.com/article/11/04/2024/an-ai-polling-startup-polls-bots-predicts-harris-will-win) of real-world media that personas would likely have [consumed](https://www.semafor.com/article/11/04/2024/an-ai-polling-startup-polls-bots-predicts-harris-will-win). Many companies offer clients the option to [integrate](https://www.electrictwin.com/#science) proprietary customer data as well, [including](https://www.simile.com/) loyalty metrics, financial balances, or telemetry data. Synthetic surveys extend the universe of simulation-based AI research, which has gained traction within experimental [physics](https://www.arenaphysica.com/publications/heaviside-1), [self-driving](https://helm.ai/) cars, and [manufacturing](https://www.wired.com/story/bmw-virtual-factory-ai-hone-assembly-line/) line optimization.

## The Synthetic Survey Landscape

Despite its infancy, there are already a variety of players in the synthetic survey landscape, each targeting slightly different approaches or swaths of customers. A review of these companies is not intended to be a competitive overview but rather to emphasize how quickly the industry has sprung up and how quickly these companies have achieved meaningful traction.

### Newcomers

**Aaru** is an AI simulation company founded in [March 2024](https://techcrunch.com/2025/12/05/ai-synthetic-research-startup-aaru-raised-a-series-a-at-a-1b-headline-valuation/) and valued at [$1 billion](https://www.natesilver.net/p/ai-polls-are-fake-polls) as of September 2026, which is focused primarily on simulation of events and behaviors rather than survey responses. A white paper on the company’s site [sets out](https://www.semafor.com/article/09/20/2024/ai-startup-aaru-uses-chatbots-instead-of-humans-for-political-polls) its ambitions: “within two years, we will simulate the entire globe — from the way crops are grown in Ukraine to how that impacts production of oil in Iraq, trade through the Strait of Malacca, and elections for the mayor of Baltimore.” Aaru’s track record of political forecasts is not impressive (it gave Harris a [50.5%](https://x.com/schaumburgd/status/1852802999250465144) chance of winning the US presidential election on November 2nd 2024, a miss Fink has [described](https://www.semafor.com/article/11/06/2024/ai-startup-aaru-defends-using-artificial-intelligence-for-polling) in saying, “Statistically speaking, we’re within the margin of error — so we did well” and “A coin flip is a coin flip; 53-47 is not significantly different from 48-52.”

As of September 2026, the company’s published list of clients and partners [includes](https://www.wsj.com/business/ai-startup-aaru-young-founders-35da7f87) businesses such as OpenAI, Accenture, Bayer, Comcast, EY, SharkNinja, Spindrift, and McDonald's. Dave Burwick, the CEO of Spindrift, has described the benefit of AI-assisted polling in [saying](https://www.wsj.com/business/ai-startup-aaru-young-founders-35da7f87), “The biggest challenge for consumer product companies is, how do you shorten that innovation cycle?” (Burwick is an [investor](https://www.wsj.com/business/ai-startup-aaru-young-founders-35da7f87) in Aaru). In 2025, Burwick [tasked](https://www.wsj.com/business/ai-startup-aaru-young-founders-35da7f87) Aaru with assessing soda, tea, energy drink, and smoothie products for a targeted demographic (25- to 35-year-old consumers with six-figure household incomes). The company’s simulations assessed fruit tea as the best opportunity, agreeing with Spindrift’s two-month real-world study of 500 human consumers. After the study, Spindrift launched an iced tea and squeezed fruit product based in part on this analysis.

Aaru has leaned [explicitly](https://aaru.com/) into the distinction between human behaviors and reported preferences; the company’s website described case studies in which humans are unreliable narrators:

**Simile** is a synthetic survey company cofounded by Joon Sung Park in [2025](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/30/synthetic-user-startup-simile-raises-200m-at-2b-valuation-5-months-after-100m-series-a/), an AI communities researcher and the [creator](https://baincapitalventures.com/insight/the-human-layer-of-ai-why-we-re-continuing-to-invest-in-simile/) of Smallville, a 2023 virtual town of generative agents that first demonstrated the architecture required to [simulate](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/computational-agents-exhibit-believable-humanlike-behavior) human individual and social behaviors in collectives. Unlike some synthetic survey companies, Simile agents map [one-to-one](https://baincapitalventures.com/insight/the-human-layer-of-ai-why-we-re-continuing-to-invest-in-simile/) to real-world individuals, grounding agent responses in answers from structured interviews with each person along with a real record of individual choices and behavioral data. This is distinct from synthetic-user products that start from a demographic profile played by a general-purpose model.

Simile raised $200 million at a [$2 billion](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/30/synthetic-user-startup-simile-raises-200m-at-2b-valuation-5-months-after-100m-series-a/) valuation in July 2026. Within five months of launching, Simile says it had [run](https://baincapitalventures.com/insight/the-human-layer-of-ai-why-we-re-continuing-to-invest-in-simile/) simulations numbering in the tens of millions for enterprises at the top of the Fortune list; the company’s website [names](https://www.simile.com/) CVS Health, Wealthfront, Suntory Beverages & Food, Gallup and Garnett Station Partners among its customers (CVS Health Ventures is also an investor in the company). The agents behind that work were built from [2.9 million](https://baincapitalventures.com/insight/the-human-layer-of-ai-why-we-re-continuing-to-invest-in-simile/) consented responses contributed by more than [400K](https://baincapitalventures.com/insight/the-human-layer-of-ai-why-we-re-continuing-to-invest-in-simile/) research participants, and CVS Health has used the platform to answer questions ranging from medication adherence to how a store should be laid out to whether a customer would give medicine to a pet.

**Artificial Societies** is a London-based synthetic survey company founded in [2024](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/artificial-societies) to [provide](https://societies.ai/) advice for strategic communications, including crisis and issue management, expansion to new markets, investor relations, and government messaging. The company was co-founded by James He, who led the first peer-reviewed [paper](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/james-k-he_our-original-33000-chatbot-society-paper-share-7439109285038596096--bFW/) on agent swarms at scale, observing how [33K](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/artificial-societies) chatbots behaved among themselves. His co-founder, former consultant Patrick Sharpe, agreed to form the company with him after seeing James simulate in [10 minutes](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/artificial-societies) the result of an experiment Sharpe had worked on for [two months](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/artificial-societies). The company uses both real-world surveys (mixed-method surveys, interactive focus groups, and interviews) in addition to multiverse experiments and scenario cascade simulation methods.

Other companies in this space include **Electric Twin** (founded in [November 2023](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/electric-twin)), **Minds** (founded in [October 2025](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/minds-7b06)), and **Evidenza** (founded in [January 2024](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/evidenza-limited)). Companies with the explicit goal of testing against synthetic audiences include **Replism** (founded in [May 2026](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/replism)) and **Deepsona** (founded in [November 2025](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/deepsona)). The track record of these firms is also meaningful: Minds [works](https://getminds.ai/) with Accenture, Canva, Deloitte, and Stripe, among other customers, and Evidenza clients [include](https://www.evidenza.ai/) ServiceNow, EY, SentinelOne, Mars, Salesforce, Toast, and SAS. [Jim Lesser,](https://www.evidenza.ai/) the Chief Brand Officer of ServiceNow, said of the service, “I'd recommend NOT working with the Evidenza Team. The technology just might be game-changing, and we'd like to keep the competitive advantage for ourselves” (Evidenza's site carries a ServiceNow case study claiming that a [year](https://www.evidenza.ai/) of conventional research was compressed into a single [month](https://www.evidenza.ai/), producing the persona work, the segmentation, and the creative brief at [12 times](https://www.evidenza.ai/) the usual pace).

### Traditional Polling

In addition to dedicated AI polling companies, traditional polling institutes are experimenting with AI-generated data panels as a supplement to human respondents. Incumbents like [Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/methodology/709373/gallup-begins-research-simulated-responses.aspx), [Qualtrics](https://www.qualtrics.com/articles/news/new-market-research-capabilities-x4-2026/), [Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/synthetic-data-boosting), and [YouGov](https://parallax.yougov.com/) are all developing such functionality.

Gallup is independently [validating](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/methodology/709373/gallup-begins-research-simulated-responses.aspx) Simile's simulated-response method. As of May 2026, its study of the method [used](https://www.fastcompany.com/91554056/synthetic-data-is-everywhere-but-is-it-any-good) agents generated based on interview data from [1K](https://www.fastcompany.com/91554056/synthetic-data-is-everywhere-but-is-it-any-good) Gallup Panel members and benchmarked agent-based results against probability-based results. Gallup's early read was that the simulated distributions sat [near enough](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/methodology/709373/gallup-begins-research-simulated-responses.aspx) to what people actually said for the work to be worth continuing, though it published no accuracy figure. Gallup has [ruled out](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/methodology/709373/gallup-begins-research-simulated-responses.aspx) using simulated responses for published estimates or tracking, and has pointed to questionnaire pre-testing and hard-to-reach populations as areas of potential value.

Qualtrics [launched](https://www.cxtoday.com/customer-analytics-intelligence/qualtrics-x4-experience-management-cx/) synthetic survey panels for US consumers in March 2026, claiming to deliver results in hours at [50%](https://www.cxtoday.com/customer-analytics-intelligence/qualtrics-x4-experience-management-cx/) the cost of human panels. The company [claims](https://itbrief.news/story/qualtrics-launches-synthetic-panels-hub-to-speed-research) that its models approximate human responses 12x better than general-purpose AI models. The synthetic survey platform offered by Qualtrics [combines](https://www.qualtrics.com/articles/news/new-market-research-capabilities-x4-2026/) synthetic and human panels to enable teams to test early ideas fast and validate later-stage decisions with real test groups. Panels for the UK and Ireland, Canada, and Australia and New Zealand [were slated](https://insightinnovationventures.substack.com/p/what-caught-our-eye-this-week-3202026) for the first half of 2026 as of March.

As of September 2026, Ipsos [focuses](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/synthetic-data-boosting) on synthetic data boosting, which enlarges real datasets when samples are small or uneven. The company [favors](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/publication/documents/2026-02/Ipsos-Update-February-2026.pdf) tabular diffusion models, which it considers steadier than the older methods. Its SURE framework [checks](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/publication/documents/2026-02/Ipsos-Update-February-2026.pdf) boosted data for statistical similarity, utility and fairness, rarity and novelty, and expert

kept.heading: WHAT WOULD A CHILD-FREE INTERNET LOOK LIKE? (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Australia's under-16 social media ban deactivated 4.7M accounts, yet more than 80% of surveyed children still used age-restricted services. A “child-free” internet could push young users toward gaming, messaging, and smaller platforms, making their activity harder to monitor. Children could also remain visible through adult-run family influencer accounts. The shift could make young consumers' influence less visible to brands while limiting children's access to online communities and digital experiences.

Title: What Would A Child-Free Internet Look Like?

URL Source: https://www.wired.me/story/what-would-a-child-free-internet-look-like

Published Time: 2026-09-21T14:31:06.612+04:00

Markdown Content:
Australia’s [under-16 social media ban](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r7284) took effect in December 2025, leading to the deactivation of roughly [4.7 million accounts](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/australia-social-media-ban-hits-47-million-teen-accounts-first-month-2026-01-15/) in its first five weeks. Yet the country’s [eSafety Commissioner](https://www.esafety.gov.au/research/social-media-age-restrictions-evaluation/early-days-early-insights-three-months-report) later reported that more than 8 in 10 children surveyed were still using at least one age-restricted service.

The idea has travelled regardless. The [UAE introduced its own restrictions in June](https://www.wired.me/story/the-uae-just-banned-social-media-for-under-15s-do-these-bans-actually-work), giving platforms 12 months to comply, while several other governments are considering similar measures.

But pushing children off major social platforms does not necessarily push them offline. It may instead relocate them to gaming, messaging and other digital spaces, encourage them to find ways around age checks, or leave them visible only through content published by adults. A child-free social internet could therefore prove less child-free than advertised.

## Where Would Children Go?

Children’s online lives already extend far beyond conventional social media. [Ofcom’s 2026 research](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/media-use-and-attitudes/media-habits-children/childrens) found that YouTube and WhatsApp were among the services most commonly used by children in the UK. Australia, meanwhile, has an estimated [1.7 million young Roblox users](https://www.roymorgan.com/findings/10136-yas-roblox-for-young-australians-survey-december-2025).

Crystal Abidin, a professor and digital anthropologist at Curtin University, says young people often establish communities in less-prominent online spaces before creators follow them there. “Young people were flocking to these spaces already to find their online communities, and then the creators followed suit,” she says.

The threatened US TikTok ban offered a glimpse of how quickly users can look elsewhere. In January 2025, shortly before TikTok briefly went dark in the US, more than half a million self-described “TikTok refugees” joined the Chinese app Xiaohongshu (RedNote), according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/over-half-million-tiktok-refugees-flock-chinas-rednote-2025-01-14/).

“It is not uncommon for young people across all language and cultural groups to be on Chinese social media,” Abidin says. As more restrictions take effect, these platforms could become more attractive to users looking beyond Silicon Valley. Global creators and celebrities are already establishing audiences there: Erling Haaland has [official accounts](https://www.wired.me/story/erling-haaland-is-everywhere-at-the-world-cup-most-of-it-is-ai) on Douyin and Weibo, while MrBeast – whose audience includes a significant number of 13- to 17-year-olds – has [opened an account](https://space.bilibili.com/1027737427?spm_id_from=333.788.upinfo.detail.click) on Bilibili, often described as China’s answer to YouTube.

“There are Japanese, Korean, Southeast Asian, really local versions of regional apps that haven’t even been considered by any of these regulations,” Abidin adds. The same possibility exists closer to home. Middle Eastern social platforms such as [Yalla](https://www.moet.gov.ae/en/w/yalla-group), or apps popular among Arabic-speaking users such as [Jodel](https://www.wired.me/story/saudi-arabias-world-cup-exit-became-an-internet-block-party), could become more relevant if younger users are pushed away from the dominant platforms – provided their own age restrictions allow it.

## The Child Creator Economy

The creator economy could also face significant changes if children are removed from major platforms. A [2023 study](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0295337) led by researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health estimated that Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube collectively earned nearly $11 billion in US advertising revenue from users under 18 in 2022. Children accounted for an estimated 41% of Snapchat’s overall advertising revenue, followed by TikTok at 35% and YouTube at 27%.

Beauty offers one particularly visible example of young users’ commercial influence. Gen Alpha has driven online hype around retailers and brands such as [Sephora](https://www.tiktok.com/discover/kids-at-sephora?lang=en) and Drunk Elephant, while [Circana research](https://www.circana.com/post/generational-impacts-on-the-beauty-industry-in-2025) found that households with children spend more on beauty products than those without.

Tween enthusiasm has also helped propel Stanley cups, Sonny Angels and Labubu through some of the internet’s most lucrative recent trend cycles. Under-16s were not their only consumers, but the content young users created, shared and engaged with helped turn the products into online phenomena. What could disappear under a ban, then, is not necessarily the demand but brands’ ability to see and reach it.

A more complicated grey area lies within the family-influencer economy. The restrictions prevent children from holding their own accounts, but do not necessarily prevent adults from publishing content featuring them. In the UAE, the Ministry of Family’s guidance on [Resolution 106 of 2026](https://uaelegislation.gov.ae/en/legislations/4506/download) says the framework allows structured participation in non-harmful content under specific conditions and makes parents responsible for supervising that activity. In other words, a child may be unable to run an account while still being the content.

“A lot of child-centred content is not produced by child-owned or child-accessed accounts anyway,” says Professor Abidin. “And that was the barometer, wasn’t it? It’s age verification based on the account owner logging on and putting something online. It’s not so much the age of the person featured in the content. So that’s a very easy loophole to get around.”

In Australia, [more than 275,000 creators](https://www.mediaweek.com.au/aimco-launches-landmark-guide-for-child-and-family-influencers) identify as parenting or family influencers – roughly one in five creators – according to Fabulate Discovery data cited by the Australian Influencer Marketing Council (AIMCO). Abidin says some influencer parents responded to the restrictions by describing children’s accounts as parent-managed or reframing them as family accounts.

Some governments are beginning to address the labour involved separately. An [Illinois law](https://www.illinoislegalaid.org/legal-information/protections-child-influencers), which took effect in 2024, entitles eligible children under 16 who appear in monetised content to a share of the earnings, held in trust until they turn 18. California and [Minnesota](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/minnesota-law-children-content-creators-monetized-videos-guards/) have since introduced similar protections.

The Gulf also has an established family-influencer economy. Public figures, including Karen Wazen, Joelle Mardinian and Kris Fade, regularly feature their children in content published through adult-owned accounts. Those accounts would not disappear under rules focused on the age of the account holder.

“The brands are the ones fuelling this industry,” Abidin says. “They finance the influencers, incentivise them to post.” Social media companies also benefit, she adds, because family influencers attract audiences and keep them on the platforms. For Abidin, brands and platforms, therefore, offer a more effective point of intervention than account-level restrictions alone.

## A Child-Free Digital Society

Sonia Livingstone, director of the [Digital Futures for Children](https://www.digital-futures-for-children.net/) centre and a member of the UK government’s independent academic panel, has described social media bans as “an admission of failure”: governments unable to regulate platforms are instead regulating children. [Research from the centre](https://www.lse.ac.uk/news/social-media-bans-risk-excluding-children-from-important-opportunities-rather-than-tackling-harms-new-report-finds) argues that blanket restrictions risk excluding children from opportunities to communicate, participate and learn without addressing the systems that expose them to harm.

Digital fluency is no longer a skill people begin acquiring at 18. Children grow up navigating online information, communities and services long before adulthood. “It is our current state of the world that we need to prepare our citizens to be digitally savvy,” Abidin says.

Removing children from major social platforms may reduce some risks, but it could also make their online lives harder for parents, researchers and regulators to see. Young users may migrate to smaller platforms, find ways around age checks or continue appearing in monetised content without controlling the accounts themselves.

A child-free internet, then, would have pretty weighty implications for digital society as we know it, barring children from making informed critical decisions on what’s right, wrong, true or false, possibly introducing them to danger elsewhere online.

kept.heading: AI AGENT CALLS THAT ARE ACTUALLY MADE BY HUMANS IN A CALL CENTER (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Meta pitched the feature publicly as AI, but internal posts describe a "human agent layer," and at least one tester only found out after the call that a person had placed it.
kept.article_text:
Title: Meta Tests Muse AI Agent Calls That Are Actually Made By Humans in a Call Center

URL Source: https://www.404media.co/meta-tests-muse-ai-agent-calls-that-are-actually-made-by-humans-in-a-call-center/

Published Time: 2026-09-22T16:33:15.000Z

Markdown Content:
Last week, Meta executives announced that its much-hyped AI agent, Muse, had a new feature: It could call businesses for you to do things like make a restaurant reservation or a haircut appointment. But in reality, Meta is testing having these calls being made by human beings in call centers, 404 Media has learned.

“We just expanded the @muse beta for outbound calls to US businesses,” Ryan Fox, the principal engineer [on Muse posted on X](https://x.com/wailord/status/2100342273854894533?ref=404media.co) on Sept. 16. [Alexandr Wang](https://x.com/alexandr_wang/status/2100349174529265967?ref=404media.co), Meta’s chief AI officer, posted “we’re expanding our phone beta for muse!”

Internally, however, the company announced the features to employees and said that it had “added a human agent layer for calls to get completed,” and that “Muse human agent calls [sic] is ready for company dogfooding,” or testing.

“Muse doesn’t just dial a number. It calls a business on your behalf, handles the conversation, completes your request, and reports back with a transcript and a summary,” the internal message board post to employees, seen by 404 Media, reads. “It also no longer works alone. Muse is now able to hand requests to a trained human agent, who places the call and works it through.”

“This is still a confidential, pre-launch product,” the post adds. “Please don’t share it, or anything it producers, with anyone outside the company.”

Once again, a core feature of a major piece of AI technology will actually just be people working in a call center, doing work that a company says AI is doing. It is not clear how often or when a call is routed to a so-called “human agent,” and when a call is done exclusively by AI.

💡

****Do you work for Meta or know anything more about Muse? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at jason.404. Otherwise, send me an email at jason@404media.co.****

The fact that human beings are involved in the call raised questions among employees, who wondered both about the privacy implications of sharing people’s call requests with other human beings as well as the perception that its AI assistant wasn’t advanced enough to do calls on its own.

“Not sure what I am missing here but why is this a ‘feature?,’ one employee wrote on Meta’s internal message board for workers. “This has potential for so much negative PR. It could portray us as ‘their AI is not good enough so they still need humans’ kind of coverage for this launch.”

That Meta is at least sometimes letting human beings read users’ chats and make phone calls on their behalf is part of a time honored tradition in which companies launch an AI product, claim that it is AI, only for it to be later learned that human beings are doing some or all of the work. And it is the latest example of a tech giant passing [potentially highly sensitive information](https://www.404media.co/inside-project-lily-the-humans-reading-your-chatgpt-chats/) to human beings; it is easy to imagine someone asking Muse to make a sensitive doctor’s appointment, for example, and the user not knowing that a human being might make that call.

In internal communications seen by 404 Media, Meta suggested to employees that potentially sensitive information shared by the user with AI — and then passed to human contractors — was still safe because the contractors had undergone “a lot of training to make sure all your data is safe and secure.” An employee commented that the training “is not a [security] mechanism.”

“This is absolutely going to create a ton of outcry if we publicly launch this as default-on. It will kill all the goodwill and organic press we’re getting from early adopters,” they wrote. “Please think about how the headlines will scream ‘Meta uses humans behind the scenes to make calls’ or ‘Muse AI is actually independent contractors’ and result in a ton of bad press about the privacy and security of our data handling […] please PLEASE do not release this as-is and at least make this a user preference if we absolutely must launch this. Please.”

Other employees who had tested the system said that it was a “bad bad idea,” and that they were not made aware that a human being did the call for them until after the call had been made: The tester “was not made aware of the caller being human and was only told after,” one employee wrote. “So they were concerned with information that they shared with the assumption that it is the secure AI which is making the call. Even with clear indication of human calling, I can think of many scenarios where I wouldn’t be comfortable with this and I am not positive about how our users will react to this.”

Various Meta employees and regular users have posted about Muse’s ability to make phone calls, and their experience with it. Ravid Shwartz Ziv, who does AI research at Meta, [posted on X](https://x.com/ziv_ravid/status/2101362331527659864?ref=404media.co) that “this week, Muse called customer service on my behalf. It navigated the phone tree, waited on hold, spoke with a human rep, and resolved the issue (worked great!). The crazy thing for me (besides that it works) is that the rep didn’t blink. Talking to a bot was completely natural to them.” Others have posted that the call function didn’t work, or that the person on the other end [hung up on the agent](https://x.com/FamousAlan/status/2101177524541866262?ref=404media.co) (some have said that Muse did what it was supposed to do).

“Internal testing, aka dogfooding, is core to the product development process. While the response from employees has been overwhelmingly positive, the entire point is to get feedback so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve features before we release them publicly,” a Meta spokesperson told 404 Media. “We’re working with merchants to continue improving this potential calling feature, and will only roll it out when it's ready and with the proper disclosures.”

Become a paid subscriber here for access to all of our articles ad-free and bonus content.](https://www.404media.co/meta-tests-muse-ai-agent-calls-that-are-actually-made-by-humans-in-a-call-center/#/portal)

About the author

Jason is a cofounder of 404 Media. He was previously the editor-in-chief of Motherboard. He loves the Freedom of Information Act and surfing.
